Few actors are needed and an assessment of the Code is a limited task, and the State Election Commission has already acted on some irregularities. Oversight of campaign data and any change to the Electoral Code are likely to be harder, and the evidence on this is thin.

The Commission, not the Government, states that access to public information improved thanks to the strategy, which set up the open data portal. The State Audit Office reports that the portal has not functioned since early 2025, in machine-translated text capped at Medium confidence, so the 2020 result is not shown to have lasted.
The Commission states the causal link directly, but in one sentence, with no measure of the improvement and no account of other factors.

The Commission states that the changes led to more complaints, but not what the changes were meant to do. More complaints could reflect more misuse or more willingness to complain, so the outcome cannot be scored as a result.
The Commission states the cause directly and an adjacent sentence links complaints to an inconsistency in the law, but it gives no figures for the complaints.

The only evidence for increased awareness is the Agency's own statement about its own law, so success cannot be judged from it. The same strategy lists low public awareness as a weakness, and the Commission found a need for awareness raising in 2023 and low awareness in 2025.
The link rests on the Agency's unmeasured claim, with no baseline and no independent evidence that the law caused any change in awareness.

The only evidence is the Agency's report, machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, so success cannot be judged from it. It reports a rise in quiz users without a current figure, and the only count found is over 50 users in 2024.
Quiz completions can only come through the tool, so the link says little about any effect beyond use of the tool, and only the Agency reports it.

Commission items moved from no further progress on the 2019 draft law in 2021, through repeated calls to adopt the law and strategy in 2022, 2023 and 2024, to adoption of the strategy in January 2025 and the law in June 2025, which the 2025 report counts as some progress. The chapter scale (limited progress 2021 to 2024, some progress 2025) is context only and was not decisive, and the improvement lies in the legal and strategic framework, since no item shows better coordination after the 2023 call, the 2024 audit finding of a Council that met once and the 2025 strategy's own description of coordination as critical. A February 2022 ITU item lists the law as existing while the Commission's 2022 report says it was still a draft, and later Commission and audit items support the draft reading; the differing dates for the Council (2019 or 2020) and the action plan's end (2027 or 2028) do not affect this value.

The Commission found the 2025 law sufficient for the Reform Agenda step, which required alignment of primary legislation only, yet says it does not fully align with the acquis and still asks the country to continue aligning; the law, strategy and competent authority are proposed as adopted and the by-laws and disclosure and crisis frameworks as proposed, and these statuses are themselves proposals for review. What remains is the outstanding NIS2 provisions and Cybersecurity Act certification alignment (last raised before the law passed), the 15 by-laws legally due within six months but not shown as adopted, the entity lists, the disclosure and crisis frameworks, working coordination, and application to the sectors the law defers until accession. The law's text is machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, and the regulator's one-line statement that the strategy is applied is government reporting without specifics, so neither is treated as closure.

The law and strategy, an operational competent authority and the NIS2 frameworks are each Reform Agenda payment steps, and NIS2 or cybersecurity legislation recurs in the Commission's key recommendations from 2022 to 2025. The issue is the legal base on which the rest of the cybersecurity theme rests. The rating rests on these EU requirements and not on the large number of national plan and audit items.

Much of what remains is drafting that the Ministry controls, and adoption followed within a year of the Reform Agenda step, which favours progress; against this, the first draft law stalled from 2019 to 2025, the Council barely functioned and no item shows the by-laws adopted after their deadline. Coordination needs many bodies, the strategy itself names political support and budget as key risks, and one reporting obligation to ENISA cannot be met outside the EU. Tractability is therefore higher for legal alignment than for coordination.

The Commission's wording is essentially unchanged across three reports, that state institutions need stronger capacity and infrastructure and the national centre more staff (2023, 2024, 2025), and its reform programme assessments repeat large or major deficiencies in 2025 and 2026, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Incident counts cannot show a trend in capacity, because reporting was not mandatory and the figures are not comparable (1,441 or 1,443 for 2020, 2,804 for 2022, about 170 in 2023 on an unstated definition). The World Bank's advanced rating and the audit's finding of poor protection are a noted difference and not a conflict, since an index of national commitments and a test of practice measure different things, and the 2024 index itself lists technical and capacity measures as areas for growth.

The latest EU items, of November 2025 and April 2026, still call for significant strengthening and report major deficiencies, while responses are proposed as adopted on paper (the law, strategy and action plan, the national and government response teams) or only planned (government data centre, secure network, security operations centre), and the disaster recovery centre is used by 3 of about 140 bodies; these statuses are themselves proposals for review. What remains is staffed and trained response teams working to the Reform Agenda standard, security officers and tested plans in institutions, and secure government infrastructure in actual use. The Reform Agenda's 2024 baseline of CERTs not operational sits against statements that MKD-CIRT is in place, possibly because the baseline means NIS2 readiness, and the audit evidence behind this finding is machine translated, capped at Medium confidence, with percentages from a survey of 18 institutions.

Operational national and government CERTs, a staffed competent authority and a secure government network are Reform Agenda payment steps, and the Commission has repeated the need for capacity in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports. The Commission's reform programme assessments also name these deficiencies, and without operating capacity the legal framework has little effect, so the issue is central to the theme. The rating does not rest on the volume of audit and action plan items.

Progress needs people the state has struggled to hire and keep (IT posts about half filled, 3 of 11 MKD-CIRT posts filled, a shortage the strategy says extends across the region), action across about 140 bodies, and budgets the strategy itself calls at risk, while the main infrastructure is at pre-feasibility stage and looks to outside funding. Past progress is weak, as most surveyed institutions had no response team five years after the previous strategy called for them, and the new 40% salary supplement is adopted with no item yet showing its effect. Strengthening MKD-CIRT alone would be more achievable than system-wide capacity, and the audit and strategy items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

The Commission has named the 5G toolbox in its recommendations in four successive reports (2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, two of these items being classified under the framework issue), and its November 2025 wording still asks the country to continue, so the default of persistent applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Legal steps did occur (2021 amendments, 2022 by-laws, the June 2025 law with supplier risk provisions), but the screening report says not all the 2021 amendments had been implemented. A reviewer could read the 2025 law as the start of improvement, but it began to apply only in June 2026 and no later EU item assesses it.

The latest EU items ask the country to continue implementing the toolbox, including assessing suppliers and restricting high-risk ones, and the Reform Agenda requires the security by-law fully implemented by December 2027; the 2025 law is proposed as adopted, the by-law and supplier assessment as proposed, and the 2021 amendments as reversed because the new law replaces them, all of which are proposals for review. What remains is adopting and applying the by-law and actually carrying out supplier risk assessments and any restrictions, since the law gives the power (machine translated, capped at Medium) but no item shows it used. The Reform Agenda's statement that the step is largely achieved sits against its own partial compliance baseline and the Commission's later wording, and it appears to rest mainly on spectrum and legislation, so it is not treated as closure; the Commission's finding that this law's reform step was not achieved concerns the Code and the Gigabit Act and not the toolbox, and the law allows 15 months for by-laws, so the finding does not decide this gap.

Toolbox compliance is a Reform Agenda step and has been named in the Commission's key recommendations in four successive reports, and the enlargement communication presents it as a basis of secure digital infrastructure. The issue is narrow, one clause among several in the chapter's key recommendation, so centrality is the weakest part of this rating and a reviewer could reasonably set Medium. The small number of items did not lower the rating, as volume is not a criterion.

Few actors are needed, mainly the regulator and the Ministry working with operators, the law already provides the power and by-laws under the 2021 amendments were reported adopted by the following year, which all favour progress. However, not all the 2021 amendments were implemented four years on, a supplier assessment planned from 2023 is not shown as done, and operators complained of having no consultation in 2021. The evidence does not show what restrictions would cost operators, so the rating is not set higher.

Training was mandatory for state administration bodies, but the State Audit Office reports just over 19,500 attendees by December 2023 against 129,374 public administration employees, about 15%, and calls the 73% from its survey of 18 institutions not a real picture, with no monitoring set up. The denominator is wider than the bodies obliged and the snapshot is ten months after the Conclusion, so the evidence shows real but well short uptake and not outright failure. This is a single independent audit and not government self-reporting, machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, and no later figure exists.

The audit counts attendance at the trainings that the Conclusion requires, so a contribution to attendance is plausible and direct. No baseline or start date separates attendance caused by the Conclusion from attendance that would have happened anyway, and the audit's further claim about awareness is not measured.

The State Audit Office found 13% of surveyed institutions had not taken the proposed measures, implying most had, but the same audit found 67% without two-factor authentication, which it calls a minimum measure, and no way of monitoring delivery; these two findings pull in different directions and are not resolved here. The percentages come from answers to a survey of 18 institutions, and the audit is independent and not government self-reporting, but it is machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

The measures were recommendations, adopted five months after MKD-CIRT first published them, and there is no baseline, so institutions reporting that they took them may have acted earlier or for other reasons. The share is self-reported to the auditor by a small sample and no monitoring exists to check it.

The Commission moved from 'yet to align' (2022) and 'further delayed' (2023) to treating the law as harmonised with the 2014 regulation and asking for the 2024 revision (2024), then to amendments transposing eIDAS 2.0, with 'some progress' for e-government and further efforts required (2025). Sources conflict on whether alignment with the 2014 regulation already existed in 2020 (screening report and 2023 strategy against the 2022 and 2023 reports), which affects the start point but not the trend. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive; the judgement rests on the issue's own items.

The law was amended in June 2025 and the Commission counted the step as achieved for Reform Agenda purposes, while saying the law does not fully align and asking for further efforts in its 2025 report; the intervention statuses used here are themselves proposals. What remains is full alignment of the partially harmonised provisions, adoption of the 14 by-laws, which no item shows as adopted, and actual application. The machine-translated law text, capped at Medium confidence, says the amendments apply only from 1 June 2027.

The updated law is a Reform Agenda payment condition, and eIDAS alignment was raised by the Commission in each report from 2022 to 2025. It is the legal base of the electronic identification theme. The rating rests on these requirements and not on the number of items, most of which are provisions of one law.

The remaining work is mainly legal drafting led by one ministry, with a gap analysis by SIGMA and a by-law roadmap already available, and the ministry met the June 2025 law deadline. Earlier delays in 2022 and 2023 and the staged by-laws, some tied to the wallet in December 2027, are the main limits.

The Commission said in 2024 that the tools were cumbersome and neither free nor user friendly, and in 2025 that they were still not, while its 2021 report recorded only a modest rise in electronic signature use. In 2026 it found the trusted list step not achieved despite the request of 30 October 2025, so steps were taken without a changed result. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive, and the 2024 audit evidence that high-level eID did not raise use is machine translated and capped at Medium.

Two providers offer advanced and qualified signature services, as the Commission reports and as the Reform Agenda step asks, but the same step is not achieved, the tools remain not free or user friendly, and the wallet and mutual recognition are still proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. The two sides conflict: North Macedonia reports the trusted list preparation complete and considers the step achieved, while the Commission says the self-assessment and published list are outstanding. What remains is inclusion in the trusted list (grace period to 31 December 2026), usable and free tools in common use, the wallet and cross-border recognition.

Joining the trusted list and implementing the wallet are Reform Agenda steps, the first with a stated payment provision, and the Commission repeated its concern about the tools in 2024 and 2025. Recognition and use are central to the electronic identification theme.

The outstanding trusted list tasks are specific and technical, and two providers have passed ministry checks, which favours progress. Use and usability need many institutions and users, the wallet depends on regional partners and the mutual recognition agreement, and the list depends on Commission assessment. The audit found failed procurement of institutional seal certificates (machine translated, capped at Medium), which is a warning on delivery.

The Commission repeated the recommendation to align with the European Interoperability Framework and the Interoperable Europe Act in near-identical terms in 2023, 2024 and 2025, which sets the persistent default under the rules. The 2025 wording ('efforts need to continue') reports no result. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive.

The only responding intervention, alignment with the framework, has proposed status at the freeze, and this status is itself a proposal, so no aligned text is shown. Items are in tension and this is not recorded in the contradictions file: the 2023 screening says the framework is aligned with framework 2.0, while the 2023 report asks for alignment with the 2017 revision and the audit (machine translated, capped at Medium) found no study confirming alignment. What remains is a national framework shown to be aligned with the current European framework and with the Interoperable Europe Act.

This is a repeated EU requirement across three reports, but no item places it in a benchmark, a Reform Agenda payment condition or the main findings list of a report. It supports the interoperability theme, yet the Commission itself treats use of the platform as the wider obstacle.

The mechanism is legal and framework alignment, which one ministry can lead without depending on others. The caution is the record: the recommendation has not moved in three years and the plan is still only stated in a government strategy.

Commission wording that few institutions use the platform runs from 2020 through 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024, which sets the persistent default; the 2025 report records only efforts and repeats the requirement. Connection and transaction figures rose (39 institutions in 2021 to 58 or 63 in 2025; 1.5 million transactions in 2022 to 8 million in 2024), and the Commission confirms the increases in 2023 and 2024, but the counts come from government documents, machine translated and capped at Medium, and most institutions remain outside. The 2020 Commission 'slight increase' and the audit's falling traffic are a noted difference of measure and period, and the chapter scale was context only and not decisive.

The platform operates and some institutions, such as customs, exchange data regularly, but the 2025 Commission recommendation still asks to complete data exchange and the responding upgrades and reforms are mainly proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. There is a confirmed contradiction: the country told the 2023 screening that the once-only principle is applied, while its 2024 Reform Agenda says institutions still do not gather evidence ex officio. What remains is regular use of the platform by the institutions obliged to use it, so that evidence is obtained ex officio as the law prescribes.

Data exchange and ex officio evidence sit in a Reform Agenda payment condition, and completing data exchange is a repeated recommendation on public administration reform in 2023, 2024 and 2025, in the main findings in the last two. It is central to the interoperability and data themes. The large number of items, mostly from one national audit, played no part in this rating.

The platform exists and the government controls it, and use has risen somewhat, which favours progress. Against that, the audit found about 1,300 obliged institutions with no costed plan, IT pay at less than half the private sector and no coordinating body, findings the 2025 strategy partly repeats (all machine translated, capped at Medium), and the Commission cites missing software and lack of will. ITU's account of a ministers' council is a noted difference over a different body, leaving how far coordination worked in practice uncertain.

NCTS Phase 5 preparation started by 2021, delays were reported in 2023 and 2024, and the system launched in January 2025, with the Commission noting 'good progress' on IT systems in 2025. The Commission's recommendation to consolidate systems repeats each year, but the stated result changed. The sub-area wording matches this issue, yet the chapter scale was context only and not decisive.

NCTS Phase 5 is live, but the 2025 screening rates alignment between low and partial, and Phase 6, the export system and ICS2 are proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is development of the remaining systems under the strategic plan, costed at about EUR 34.5 million, with full alignment planned for 2026 to 2030.

E-customs steps appear in the Reform Agenda with a stated payment provision for Phase 6, and the customs IT recommendation recurs from 2021 to 2025, in the main findings in 2024 and 2025. The Commission calls alignment on accession critical to EU financial interests and security, so the issue is central to Chapter 29. Some Reform Agenda items carry a theme_doubtful flag because their wording stresses efficiency, not connection to the EU.

One capable agency leads, and it has delivered NCTS Phase 5 after delay and kept Phase 4 running satisfactorily. The limits are IT staffing, the planned 15 experts not yet shown as hired, cost, and an EU-driven timetable to 2030.

The requirements on ECRIS, the Visa Information System and Eurodac come essentially from one 2023 screening report, so there is no repeated or changed wording to compare. The 2021, 2022 and 2024 items concern a Frontex biometric plan and do not show whether readiness moved. The chapter scale was context only and not decisive.

Responding interventions are proposed or lack a clear status, and these statuses are themselves proposals; part of the requirement falls due only at accession, and Eurodac access before accession has no legal basis, so 'open' does not by itself mean late. What remains is a functional criminal records system with ECRIS analysis done, the technical adaptations for the Visa Information System, an IT structure compatible with Eurodac on accession, and the funding for them.

The systems matter for Chapter 24, but support is thin: one screening report states the requirements and no item shows a benchmark, Reform Agenda condition or repeated key recommendation. This is central with thin support.

Progress depends on the EU: the Commission says EU law gives candidates no Eurodac access, and the country reports it cannot build to Eurodac without the technical specifications and struggles to secure funding. The Frontex plan offers a route for border systems, but no item shows it being carried out.

The sectors do not share one trend, so this rests on those with repeated wording: CECIS from 2020 to 2025 (with 'no progress' in 2023), the business registers link from 2023 to 2025, and EU tax systems and own resources in 2024 and 2025. Some areas are better, including the 2021 COVID certificate alignment and food safety tools in 2025, which the residual label hides. The chapter scales were context only and not decisive.

The latest Commission items still ask for the CECIS link, business register readiness, tax interoperability and the own resources system, and the responding interventions are nearly all proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals. North Macedonia states it is technically ready for BRIS, but the Commission says machine-readable data alignment is still needed. What remains is connection to those systems, noting that BRIS and the Internal Market Information System also depend on EU decisions or accession.

Each requirement is repeated, and tax interoperability reaches the main findings in 2024 and 2025 and CECIS is an issue for immediate attention in 2024, but none is central to the theme as a whole and the only Reform Agenda references are railway and freight outputs in the government's text. This is a residual group spanning several chapters, so the rating is an average that would differ by sector.

The sectors differ: food safety shows active use of EU tools, the CECIS link looks technically limited yet has not been finished in over five years, and BRIS requires full company law alignment and access to groups open only to Member States and EEA countries. The rating is a mid-point, not a uniform finding.

The Commission, independent of the government, states the roll-out increased opportunities for direct and secure counter-terrorism exchange, and a later report records 387 messages exchanged. The outcome is narrow: it concerns one channel and says nothing about readiness for EU large-scale systems.

The source attributes the outcome directly to the roll-out, and this exchange channel could not exist without it. There is no baseline for message volumes, so the attribution covers the opportunity and not the amount of exchange.

The conclusions aimed to connect about 1,300 institutions, and the audit found only six new requests and no resourcing analysis or timeframe. The only outcome evidence is a State Audit Office report, which the register files under the government family: it is external audit and not government self-reporting, but the reviewers should confirm that reading, and it is machine translated and capped at Medium. Connections rose later, but the Commission still found most institutions not using the platform in 2023, and the audit came about a year after the conclusions. The State Audit Office is treated as independent, as validated at G2.

The audit links the two only by sequence. It separately gives other reasons for non-use, namely lack of IT staff, legal restrictions and missing strategies, so the low response cannot be tied to the conclusions themselves.

The Commission records two providers accredited in 2021 and still offering advanced and qualified signatures, so the immediate outcome occurred. The wider result is weaker: the tools are still not user friendly or free, and the trusted list step is not achieved.

The Commission says accreditation was based on the 2019 framework, which supports a contribution. The accreditations were obtained in two Member States and depended on the providers' own decisions, so the law was not the only factor.

Same issue and same mechanism (MEC-01): the Commission's 2007 wording on non-discrimination and permits for EU workers matches the requirement on North Macedonia, and Croatia is the only case where legal alignment was recorded as completed. The context differs: the evidence is from 2007 to 2015, Croatia was close to accession, and the EU worker provisions read here sit in one Aliens Act, while whether other laws were also changed is not known. Relevance is about the match only; the absence of outcome evidence is recorded in the case and not reflected in this rating.

Same issue and mechanism in a current accession country: new Article 178a gives EU nationals employment on the same conditions as nationals, against the requirement that North Macedonia ensures unrestricted access by accession, though the timing of Article 178a is unknown. The quota carve-out is only a neighbouring RI-FMW-002 match, on which the Commission's request (MKD-EU-2025-003-0028) conflicts with North Macedonia's own account (MKD-EU-2025-003-0010), and the Commission does not describe Montenegro's restrictions in detail. The context differs, with a closing benchmark whose terms are not public (LIM-0028) and one foreigners law; relevance is about the match only, and High or Medium is for the analyst at G6b.

The problem matches closely in substance: the Commission says Serbia's EU citizens are covered by the rules for third-country nationals and that North Macedonia's law does not distinguish them from other foreigners, though no Serbian item addresses North Macedonia's reserved private sector posts. No reform aimed at EU workers' access is visible in what was read, while the content of the 2017, 2018 and 2019 amendments is largely unread and a secondary study mentions posting of EU workers, so the case shows a stalled position and no route to closing the gap. Serbia's negotiating context on this issue is not in the evidence.
Government reporting alone with no measure, machine translated, so success is not judged.
No measure of the outcome exists to attribute.

Moldova has the closest lever to the question, a legal duty and sanctions behind an existing platform, and the agency named resistance from data owners in 2020. But no extracted item shows current underuse, the Commission reports searched in full do not name MConnect, and the audit that might address it is blocked. Coordination and capacity appear in general audit findings, not tied to platform use.

Serbia matches on the procedural duty, the exchange system and the ex officio problem. It differs in that connection is widening and the evidence is about citizens' experience, not whether institutions use the platform. Commission wording on fragmented responsibilities (SRB-EU-2025-001-0008) is in the unmatched queue and is not relied on.

Montenegro matches North Macedonia on stated institutional obstacles (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0065), and on a platform where access and active exchange are counted (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0186, MKD-EU-2023-003-0040). Commission wording on once-only has no match on the North Macedonian side, where the term appears only in the country's own screening presentation (MKD-EU-2023-003-0029), although its Reform Agenda says institutions do not gather evidence ex officio (MKD-GOV-2024-001-0097). It differs in a smaller count of institutions, a platform reported as under development in 2025 and established in 2026, no evidence of underuse by connected institutions, and resources appearing through staffing of the inspection, not IT staff in institutions.
Government reporting alone, with no method or comparison group, so success is not judged. The period is also before the run's window.
The source asserts the cause and the mechanism is direct, but nothing tests the figure.
Government reporting alone with no measure. WeBER's survey on documents resubmitted is not about the Bus, so it neither confirms nor refutes this.
No measure of the outcome exists to attribute.
Government reporting alone on one named procedure, so success is not judged.
No measure of the outcome exists to attribute: the source names the system as the cause for this procedure, as a government statement with no figure.
Government reporting alone on one named procedure, so success is not judged.
No measure of the outcome exists to attribute: the Bus is named as the channel, the source credits eEnrolment, and there is no figure.
Government reporting alone with no figure, so success is not judged. It sits against 0% of e-services querying more than one register and the Commission's finding of incomplete integration.
No measured outcome exists to attribute.

The item states a need, for standardised delivery and for monitoring how services are provided to ensure compliance with legal requirements; it is not a tested lesson. It could apply if a body monitors compliance with North Macedonia's Law on General Administrative Procedure, under which its Reform Agenda says institutions do not gather evidence ex officio (MKD-GOV-2024-001-0097). It addresses compliance with once-only, not platform use directly.

The item states a recommendation to Serbian bodies, inferred from a survey, to raise citizens' awareness of once-only, with no tested mechanism. North Macedonia's stated barriers on this issue are institutional, such as IT staff, software and process change, so the agent infers that awareness among citizens would not reach them; no North Macedonian evidence on citizen awareness is cited. It could matter only as a separate citizen-side measure.

Moldova shows the same mechanism as North Macedonia (MEC-11), with the only portfolio-wide service-level use data in the three cases, though these date from 2022. The Commission still named low demand in 2025, the same report that says access and use 'significantly increased', and the agency's 71% of requests online in 2026 is unverified, so the later reported rise qualifies the match without removing it. The context differs: EVO is described as a modular front end over the portal with a recent, untested single-portal claim, a long donor project and a dedicated agency.

Albania matches on one portal, depth of transactions, inclusion and coordination (MEC-08), but it differs on the core symptom because reported use is high, not low. It is a contrast case for consolidation and for range as the Commission reports it, although the RCC says Albania lags the regional average on service scope and sophistication (50 against 53), and it cannot explain what produces use.

Montenegro is the closest match in problem: a live portal, too few transactional services, low use, services run outside the portal and capacity limits (MEC-03, MEC-11). The match is on the problem and not on a solution, because the results are too early and unverified and its portal is newer than North Macedonia's.
The figure comes from the agency's page, quoting the project's funder, with no base or survey named. The Commission's general statement that use increased is not tied to this project.

The indicator counts any online contact with authorities (ALB-IO-2026-001-0046), so the figure cannot show a result of this portal. The Commission's request and the monitor's report on payment concern access and payment, not this outcome, so they do not make it mixed.
The RCC says the uptake is closely linked to the portal, but gives no test and does not separate the law, closed counters or pre-filled forms.
This is a statement of association, with no figure of its own. It says nothing of how far services were transacted in full.
The statement is untested and does not mention the law or the closed counters.

Closing counters is a change in how services are provided, and the source gives no count, date or effect on users. Another passage says municipal offices still handle in-person steps, and the two are not reconciled.

The civil society monitor (independence rated partly, SQ-00144) states this result directly, but only for one overlap on monitoring, evaluation and reporting between ADISA and the Agency for Dialogue and Co-governance. Informants add that ADISA's effectiveness reportedly declined after digitalisation, and it says nothing about use.
The monitor names the change directly, for one overlap between two bodies, but gives no before-and-after measure.

The result is a null on the service delivery grades, but the monitor's findings run to the end of 2024, when the portal was under construction, with later notes to July 2025, so the grades largely predate the first services of April 2025. The government reports 106 services since, with no later check outside government. 'Failed' would be too strong on this timing.

The monitor gives its reason directly, that the sampled services are not on the portal, but the grades largely predate the first services, so timing is another available explanation. It also rests on one monitor and a sample of seven.

The non-government monitor, co-funded by the ministry, states an improvement in information only, at the time of writing, while data on services were still being collected. It says nothing about transactions or use. The same organisation's event report (MNE-CSO-2025-002-0011) repeats the claim and is counted once here.
The link is direct, but it rests on one organisation and gives no before-and-after measure.

This is government reporting alone, and the improved user experience has no measure. The same source puts satisfaction at about 50%, and the government's own Digital Services Plan, as cited by the monitor, puts no service at level 5, which is not an outside check.
Outputs are attributable on the government's account, but the improved experience is asserted without any measure to which a contribution could be attached.

The source states that launch does not bring use, which matches North Macedonia's record of 292,179 users with 2,070 monthly applications. It transfers on condition that North Macedonia's low use has the same character, services available but unused, which its figures suggest but do not show service by service; it does not say what would raise use.

The item states a lesson: building without beneficiaries' opinions harms use, which the brief asserts without a test. It applies on condition that user involvement is part of design and that the services people want exist. North Macedonia's Reform Agenda prioritises usability, but the cited item says nothing about consulting beneficiaries, so the first condition is unmet at present.

The item states a general lesson drawn from Montenegro's record, that digitalisation is a matter of political will and institutional capacity. The transfer holds for capacity only, on condition that North Macedonia's unfilled posts and fragmented ownership are tackled along with the technology; the cited items do not support political will, which is insufficient_evidence. The event report is rated Low and gives no proof; item 0016 assigns the same sentence to a ministry official, but the source shows the report's closing line, to correct at the gate.

Croatia said in 2007 that the Act had been in force since 1 January 2004 and that foreigners work under it with permits. No extracted item states its status after 2007, and no extracted item connects it to the Act repealed by NN 130/2011.

The only evidence is an unofficial free excerpt, marked as the OG 74/13 text, saying the Act transposes Directive 2004/38/EC. It does not include the EU chapter, and no extracted item shows that chapter in use.

The Act was passed on 28 October 2011 and entered into force on 1 January 2012, with Articles 153 to 203 entering into force on accession. No extracted item shows those provisions being applied after accession, so implemented and in_practice are not supported. Adoption rests on the Official Gazette text alone, and later amendments were not checked.
Croatia said in 2007 that it planned to amend the Act on Employment Mediation and Unemployment Rights before the end of 2007. No later extracted item states whether this happened.

Croatia said in 2007 that amendments were being prepared to abolish work permits for EU nationals. No extracted item states their adoption, and none connects them to NN 130/2011 or the earlier act it repeals.

The Commission states that amendments to the Aliens Act were adopted to align with Directive 2004/38/EC from accession, with no year or Gazette reference. Its report is dated 12 October 2011, before NN 130/2011 was passed on 28 October 2011, and that text is a new Act repealing the earlier one (HRV-GOV-2011-001-0007), so these amendments are an earlier unidentified text. No extracted item shows them applied.

The transitional arrangement is an EU treaty term, not a Croatian national measure; the Commission recorded in 2012 that Croatia may apply equivalent measures and in 2015 that it had done so, and Article 236 ties national use to the duration of Member States' measures. A treaty end date of 30 June 2020 is recorded in a queued item (HRV-EU-2015-001-0002) that is not used under G5b, so no usable item states its position at the context date. Whether to release that item is raised at G6b.

The Commission stated in 2015 that Croatia requires a work permit from nationals of restricting Member States, so the measure was in practice then, though the source gives no figures. Article 236 ties the measure to the duration of Member States' measures, and a treaty end date of 30 June 2020 is recorded in a queued item (HRV-EU-2015-001-0002) that is not used under G5b. No usable item states whether it continues at the context date, and whether to release that item is raised at G6b.
The exemption for key staff appears only in Croatia's own 2007 account, and no later extracted item mentions it.

The law was adopted on 31 December 2025 and entered into force on 17 January 2026, the date resting on a law firm note; named clauses apply only from accession, the amending law does not say when Article 178a applies, the base law's commencement clauses were not read, and no secondary acts are in the extracted items. The Government says implementation continued and that applying the law improved procedures, including on EU nationals' rights (MNE-GOV-2026-003-0013; MNE-GOV-2026-003-0014), but this is a machine-translated, uncorroborated self-report naming no clause, and the 638 permit count does not name the law, so neither shows the measure in use. Adopted is kept, and whether the self-report is enough for implemented on the non-deferred clauses is for the analyst at G6b.
The Commission reported early preparations for amendments in 2025. A law on the same subject (INT-MNE-0002) was then adopted, but no extracted item says the preparations became that law.

The act applied from 1 February 2024; the Commission said in 2024 that the system had yet to be fully operational and in 2025 that the procedure had been simplified by it. The 2024 permit count does not name the single permit, and no extracted item gives usage or processing data, so in_practice is not supported. It concerns foreigners generally, not equal treatment of EU workers.
A secondary study states the amendments were made to simplify work permit procedures. It rests on 2018 and 2019 papers, and no extracted item shows their effect in use.

Serbia's own account in 2015 states that the Labour Law, last amended in 2014, prohibits discrimination including on nationality. No extracted item shows it applied to EU workers' access to employment, and the Commission's finding of misalignment comes from the same report.

The law was adopted in November 2014, and the Commission reports work permits in 2023 and 2024, but those counts do not name this law and the 2024 count may fall under the amended regime, so in_practice is not supported and implemented is the most that can be proposed. This does not cover the free-access clause for EU citizens, which by Serbia's account takes effect only on accession, so it is not yet applicable. Whether that clause survives is unknown.
The law is named once, in Serbia's own 2015 account, as setting conditions under which a foreigner can work. No later extracted item addresses it.
The observatory records a launch in December 2020 with 11 data blocks, and the agency lists an update. Its use statement gives no source, so in_practice is not supported.
The Interoperable Europe supporting document states the Citizen Portal launched in October 2020, and the agency lists an update to it. No item classified to this issue measures its use.

The agency's notice says the Code was amended, effective 18 January 2021. A full-text search of the Moldovan sources held shows no data exchange provision applied, and the base Code is not itself a reform of this issue.

The agency's notice states the Article 250 1 sanctions and their effective date. A full-text search of the Moldovan sources held shows no fine or disqualification applied, so adoption is all that can be said.

Interoperable Europe describes the portal as a single point of entry, and the agency lists an update to it. The user satisfaction figure comes from a government project survey, so in_practice is not proposed, and the portal is peripheral to this issue.

Interoperable Europe states that Law 142/2018 defines data exchange through MConnect, and the agency's notice names the law as where the obligation was laid down. Whether its duties are observed is not shown.

The agency's notice states that the duty was written into Article 6, effective 18 January 2021. A full-text search of the Moldovan sources held shows nothing on whether authorities have stopped asking for documents.
The Court of Accounts names MCloud among the government platforms, and the agency lists an update to it. No item classified to this issue measures its use.

The platform runs, but regular use rests only on the operator's own figures and descriptions, which are not enough for in_practice. The one independent source records a named connection under analysis and no evidence of a planned exchange working, and it is not an audit of MConnect.

Among extracted items, named only in the agency's project summary as a new platform, a government self-report of output. No item classified to this issue shows use, and it is peripheral to this issue.

Among extracted items, named only in the agency's project summary as a new platform, a government self-report of output. No item classified to this issue shows use, and it is peripheral to this issue.
The Court of Accounts names MPass among the government platforms, and the agency lists an update to it. No item classified to this issue measures its use.
The agency lists an update to MPay and claims savings from it, both self-reported. This is not enough for in_practice, and MPay is peripheral to data exchange.

Among extracted items, named only in the agency's project summary as a new platform, a government self-report of output. No item classified to this issue shows use, and it is peripheral to this issue.

The agency lists an update, and the Court of Accounts names it among the government platforms (machine translated, capped at Medium, outside LIM-0029 as worded, for the analyst to confirm at G6b). The brief's barrier concerns signatures generally. The Commission's e-signature user figures (200,000 and over 266,000) do not name MSign and sit in the unmatched queue (MDA-EU-2024-001-0006, MDA-EU-2025-001-0006), so they stay unused and are listed for the analyst.
The only item concerns connecting SIA Colaborator to MConnect, which the ministry told the Court was under analysis. No extracted item says how far the system itself operates.

The Court of Accounts discusses SIA REA as a party to planned exchange, was shown no evidence that the exchange was carried out or works, and found no concrete results from related actions in 2021 to 2022. Its own operating status is not stated in these items.
The SIERUSS Concept provides for exchange with SIA REA through MConnect, but the Court of Accounts was shown no evidence that this was carried out or is functional.

Among extracted items, named only in the agency's project summary as a new platform serving MConnect, a government self-report of output. No extracted item shows whether the catalogue changed use of the platform.

Interoperable Europe describes the date.gov.md portal as a one-stop shop for public sector data, and the agency's 2020 slides show access running through it; no item measures its use, so in_practice is not proposed. Judged separately, the authorised access route for participants with no system is stated in 2020 with a Notary Chamber case study title, and no later source text searched confirms that it operates.

Among extracted items, named only in the agency's project summary as a new platform, a government self-report of output. No item classified to this issue shows use, and it is peripheral to this issue.

The Commission confirms the improved Bus launched in December 2023 and that more databases are connected, but gives no volume of use. The volume figures are the Ministry's own, and WeBER's sampled services do not name the Bus, so in_practice is not proposed; the analyst may weigh this differently.
The Commission states in 2024 and 2025 that the framework is in place. Being in place says nothing on use.

CONFLICT: WeBER says its research confirmed the once-only principle is implemented in sampled services except property registration, with a score of 3/3, but also that it is not applied consistently, and around 53 to 54% report submitting documents already held, against 68% agreeing in general and a citizen experience score of 0.5/2. The Serbian report says points come from observing sample services but not what was observed for the 3/3, and on the same indicator the Montenegrin report gives points because document lists are published (MNE-CSO-2025-001-0026), so nothing shows exchange observed in practice. WeBER is a civil society monitor with the Ministry as project associate; Tier 3 because of the conflict.

WeBER, a civil society monitor with the Ministry as project associate, names the eDesk service and states that property registration now has to be obtained through lawyers and geodetic organisations using it, so in_practice is kept although no count of use is given. It says nothing on whether once-only applies there.
The Ministry says enrolment now runs without paper documents, with the school obtaining them through the Bus. This is government reporting alone, so in_practice is not proposed.

The RCC describes the strategy as in place, and the ministry's report on its action plan gives 43.14% of planned 2024 activities fulfilled (machine translated, whole strategy and not only e-services), which the monitor repeats. That is partial delivery on the government's own report with no measure of use, so it is implemented and not in_practice. Item MNE-GOV-2025-002-0007 was classed out_of_scope at pass 2 (LIM-0026), for the analyst to confirm at G6b.

An official says the goal of strengthening the inspection was not achieved because of delays in the staffing plan. No extracted item says what the inspection does now, or whether it has acted on data exchange.

JSERP operates and the Commission reports some progress on data exchange in 2024, but it also says register integration is incomplete in 2025. Direct figures on platform use are government self-reports and no source text searched measures platform use from outside government; the Regional Cooperation Council's pre-filled forms score is a proxy that does not name JSERP. So in_practice is not proposed.
The Commission treats the law as in application but says in 2024 and 2025 that it is not implemented consistently, notably on once-only and electronic communication.

The Regional Cooperation Council describes the law as the legal basis for modernisation, and an official says some public bodies are not meeting their obligations under it. No extracted item shows how far it is applied.

Government sources describe the Metaregister with counts of 45, 170+ and 265 that may measure different things. No source text searched reports its contents or use from outside government: a speaker at the Institute Alternative event calls it the foundation for e-services (no item extracted), which does not show use, and a catalogue is not evidence of use.
The items present the action plan and its targets as proposed for 2026 to 2029. No extracted item records adoption.

The RCC refers to the strategy as existing and does not say adopted, and the Commission says its implementation 'is improving but not yielding the expected results yet'. That wording is chapter-wide, and no extracted item gives the strategy's adoption date or its delivery on the portal.

The Commission says the government should work on transactional services through the Reform Agenda, and the monitor says the Agenda sets delivery of user-friendly digital public services, starting with the Digital Services Plan 2025-2027. That shows the reform set and not delivered; delivery is assessed under INT-MNE-0014, and no extracted item gives the Agenda's adoption date.

The sources differ in kind on the launch: the government adopted an information note in December 2024 when the monitor says the portal was not functional, the Commission and the event report say it launched that month, and first services came in April 2025. The government reports 106 services (machine translated). No extracted item gives use of the portal, and none of the sampled services was on it, so a live system is not shown to be used.

CONFLICT: Institute Alternative scores practice 3/3, but on the basis of published document lists (MNE-CSO-2025-001-0026), while citizen experience scores 0/2 and the Commission says once-only is not consistently applied. Nothing observes exchange in practice, so no status is forced; Tier 3 because of the conflict.
The agency reports an annual survey run for the project, and results are published. This is a monitoring tool, and its evidence is the agency's own.
The observatory describes the page as a monitoring tool. No extracted item shows anyone using it to act on the data.

The brief states that the Government approved the strategy on 14 September 2023, and the Commission says the government 'remained committed to implementing' it (2024) and 'continued to implement' it with 'notable progress' on all key performance indicators (2025). This wording is chapter-wide, and both items carry no issue under the G5 ruling. The 75% target for end-2024 stands against 70% reported in 2026, and no extracted item measures use, so the status stops at implemented.

The Commission records the launch in June 2024, describing it as a digital identity wallet, while the agency calls it the single portal and lists all services regardless of how they are provided. No extracted item gives EVO use, and the in_practice description comes from government and an observatory summary, so it is not enough for in_practice.
The Commission reports services launched on this platform in two reports. The term is generic, and no extracted item measures its use.
A civil society brief describes the ministry's platform and what it shows. No extracted item shows it being used.
The only item, from 2023, says it is in the process of implementation and launch, and no later extracted item says whether it launched.
STISC data, reported in the brief, give 18,400 and 17,725 active certificates in September 2022. These are certificates held at an old date and not evidence of use for services.
The agency reports the project as concluded, with a closing event and listed outputs. Results rest on the agency and the funder, so in_practice is not supported.

The Commission confirms 83 centres in 2023 and 105 in total, providing access for rural people, and the agency says they are functional. No extracted item gives how many people used them, so the status stops short of in_practice.
The data reported in the brief show 66 certificates on eID cards in September 2022, so the measure existed. That number is too small and too old to support in_practice.
The agency refers to two projects implemented over 15 years and credits this one with shared savings. It is the only evidence, and it gives no detail of the project.

The monitor records the closure and abolition of ADISA, which meets 'withdrawn' in the extraction rules for the agency itself, with its functions taken over under INT-ALB-0002. The reversal is of the body, not of one-stop delivery. The analyst may prefer to hold ADISA only as an actor, as the entity note says.

The civil society monitor, whose independence is rated partly because it names the implementing agency as a partner (SQ-00144), states that the National Agency for Information Society now holds policy and operational control and that the absorption resolved one named overlap. It gives no date and no measure of the arrangement in use, so in_practice is not supported.
The monitor says the Code institutionalises the one-stop-shop model under Article 74. No extracted item shows the article itself being applied.
The Commission says the agenda is being implemented and progressing, while equal access remains an issue. Its outcomes as such are not measured against its own targets.

The RCC and the monitor describe the platform connecting registries and supporting pre-filled data, but neither gives a measure of its use, so it stops at implemented, as INT-MNE-0020, INT-MNE-0021 and INT-MDA-0015 do. Queue items ALB-CSO-2025-001-0010 and ALB-CSO-2025-001-0065 (half of surveyed citizens on documents the state holds) bear on this, but stay unused under G5b and are listed for the analyst.

Adoption in June 2023 and the duties are clear, and the one duty traced to practice in the usable items, e-payment, is reported as limited. The monitor also reports the once-only duty both ways, as 'effectively implemented' (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0017) and as partial (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0010, ALB-CSO-2025-001-0057, ALB-CSO-2025-001-0059, ALB-CSO-2025-001-0065), but these are queue items, unused under G5b and listed for the analyst. 'Implemented' would follow only if the analyst releases those items or reads portal consolidation as application of the law, which no extracted item states.

An order of 9 June 2023 set up the working group and the agency reports reorganisation under way with 14 institutions, both on the agency's account, but the monitor states that no service has been implemented as a life event. It remains in progress and not delivered.

The Commission, the monitor and the RCC all describe the portal as the single point of contact in use, and the RCC reports volumes. The volumes are not of known origin, and the status says nothing about how far services are fully transactional.
The monitor records a chatbot on the portal. No extracted item shows how much it is used or whether it helps.
The only item lists service passports among measures outlined in the strategy. No extracted item shows them delivered.
The government states the project produced over 45 services and the portal. This is government reporting, and the same source says citizens and businesses have not fully exploited them.
In July 2025 the ministry says the law was awaited, and no later item records adoption.

The monitor records the ePayment portal as introduced, and 1,070 transactions in 2024 from the government's report, in item MNE-CSO-2025-001-0015, which pass 2 classed out_of_scope (LIM-0026) because e-payment is not a case issue. That is a small count from a government source, and the same monitor calls systems of this kind lacking in function.

CONFLICT: The government reports 25 of 57 planned 2025 services in July 2025 and then 57 of 57 (self-reported and machine translated), while the organiser's conference report, dated 2025 and possibly before that delivery, says citizens still lack real electronic services, and no extracted item confirms that the 57 are transactional. The 57 are only the 2025 tranche of a plan for 171 services to 2027 (162 in the RCC, 175 in the revised plan's table), revised on 18 December 2025. The plan is adopted, but delivery cannot be settled from these items, so the status is for the analyst.
The ministry says it upgraded the catalogue module in 2023, but also that institutions do not publish their services on it. The Commission finds no user-friendly central catalogue.
The non-government monitor, co-funded by the monitored ministry, says some services are provided through this portal. No extracted item gives use figures, so the status stops short of in_practice.
