The Parliament decision approving the cybersecurity policy document is referred to as a draft, and no source reports its adoption.
The Government describes the programme's action plan, including re-engineering of the electronic procurement system. No source reports how far it has been carried out.
The decision on connecting the National Vehicle Register to EUCARIS appears only as a draft in the 2025 accession programme, and no source reports its approval.
The Government reports that the amendments to Law No. 220/2007, together with the State Register of Legal Units, partially transpose the EU rules on digital tools in company law.
Training of health professionals in e-health is planned for 2027, and no source reports it carried out.
The amendment to Government Decision No. 211/2019 on MConnect appears as a planned act in the 2025 accession programme, and no source reports its approval.
Telemedicine and remote consultation services are a planned action, and no source reports a platform launched.
Digitalising social and employment services is set out as a priority, and no source reports specific measures carried out.
Connection to the CCN Gateway is a planned action with the indicator of an operational connection, and no source reports it achieved.
The network code on cybersecurity of cross-border electricity flows is listed for transposition, and no source reports an ANRE decision adopted.

The climate monitoring, reporting and verification system with digital registers is planned, and no source reports it developed.

Developing the eArhiva information system is a planned action, and no source reports it developed.

The National Accession Programme plans transposition actions on electronic identification and trust services for 2025 and 2026, and these items do not report them completed.

The National Employment Agency reports career guidance through the Cognitrom platform for 1,538 people. This rests on the Agency's own reporting.
The National Employment Agency reported the referral platform as under development and planned to be functional in the second half of 2025. No later source reports it launched.
The Government reports that Government Decision No. 66/2026 establishing the Government Customer Support Service was approved at the beginning of 2026. No source reports the service working.
The Government reports that registration of independent economic activity is available online through the Public Services Agency portal and the EVO application. No source gives data on its use.
The Government reports that the law on testing and innovation spaces in AI and data governance is being drafted.
The Government reports that nine services from the State Fiscal Register are available to local authorities through the external registers module. This rests on government reporting.
The Government reports that Government Decision No. 319/2025 approved the concept of the Real Estate Cadastre information system and the regulation of its information resource.
The only item refers to the list of medium-term policy priorities for 2027 to 2029 and its AI priority but does not say whether the list has been approved.

The National Employment Agency reports an automated question-answering tool designed under the I-PATH project with CEDA and the Norwegian Refugee Council. This rests on the Agency's own report, which gives no data on its use.

The Government reports that amendments to Article 2(1) of Law No. 274/2011, applicable from March 2026, entitle EU, EEA and Schengen citizens with a residence card to integration measures, including ANOFM services. No source yet reports their application.
The Government's page on bilateral agreements lists the agreement with Austria together with its administrative arrangement and forms. It gives no date of entry into force or data on its use.
The Government's page on bilateral agreements lists the agreement with Czechia together with its arrangement and forms. It gives no date of entry into force or data on its use.
The Government's page on bilateral agreements lists the agreement with Luxembourg together with its arrangement and forms. It gives no date of entry into force or data on its use.

The National Centre for Personal Data Protection reports that in 2025 it focused on drafting guidelines on applying Law No. 195/2024, but does not say whether they were issued.

The only item is the data protection authority's recommendation to amend fiscal legislation on the use of personal identification numbers on receipts, which gives no evidence on the status of any change.
The data protection authority reports its final approved budget for 2025 under the State Budget Law as MDL 12,705.6 thousand.
The Cyber Security Agency reports that domain names in Moldova's internet address space were scanned and monitored continuously in 2025. This rests on the Agency's own report.
The Cyber Security Agency reports that it became a member of the European Cyber Security Organisation on 25 June 2025.

The Cyber Security Agency reports that cooperation with the United Kingdom brings technical support from BAE Systems for developing and operationalising the national CSIRT. This rests on the Agency's own report.
The Cyber Security Agency reports that it held the two-day Moldova Cyber Security Forum in April 2025, including a capture-the-flag exercise.
The Government reports that a track in E-Legiferare was created to monitor its legislative initiatives through Parliament and the President. No source gives data on its use.
The regulator describes a temporary roaming tariff reduction mechanism that applied in 2024 and 2025 and was followed by Moldova's entry into Roam Like at Home on 1 January 2026.
The regulator reports that Board Decision No. 10 of 18 April 2025 approved the regulation on monitoring the use of radio frequencies.
The regulator reports that Board Decision No. 46 of 17 November 2025 approved the general licence conditions for using numbering resources.
The regulator reports that it repeatedly measured mobile coverage and quality under the methodology approved by Board Decision No. 27 of 23 August 2024. This rests on the regulator's own report.
The regulator states that it is stepping up information campaigns on consumer rights and Roam Like at Home rules, but gives no detail of campaigns carried out.
The regulator reports that Board Decision No. 45 of 17 November 2025 approved the procedure for granting the right to use technical resources.
An international partner reports that the Government adopted the National Plan "Building a European Moldova" in 2023, with digitalisation as its fifth priority. No source reports on its delivery.
An international partner reported in 2024 that the ministry was working on a long-term plan for the digital economy for 2025 to 2030, and no source reports it adopted.
An international partner describes the base registers, with MConnect, as a centralised means of accessing public data, while noting that some challenges remain.
An international partner describes the Digital Moldova page as a tool for monitoring the progress of digitalisation. No source gives data on its use.
The only item is an international partner's recommendation to adopt a National AI Strategy, and no source reports Moldovan action on it.
The only item is an international partner's recommendation to integrate Moldova's data infrastructure with the CEF Digital programme, and no source reports any participation.
The only item is an international partner's recommendation to introduce fast-track diploma recognition, and no source reports any such programme.
A research source reports that in April 2023 participating EU Member States announced the deployment of a Cyber Rapid Response Team to Moldova. No source reports the team's work.
A 2025 doctoral thesis cites Law No. 1216/1992 on state fees, as amended by Law No. 452 of 28 December 2023, as setting the fee for the right to work. No source reports how it is applied.
The Commission reports that the Council adopted in 2025 the decisions granting mutual roaming access for Moldova from 1 January 2026, and that Moldova joined Roam Like at Home on that date.

The only item is a general Commission statement that digital innovation hubs and cooperation on high-performance computing and AI are helping enlargement partners, and it does not describe cooperation with Moldova specifically.

SIGMA found in 2023 that MConnect is a well-functioning data exchange platform used by a large number of public and private organisations, and the Commission reports systems such as social assistance integrated into it. Government figures put use at about 1.5 million successful queries a day across 144 state and 252 private systems. The data protection authority found in 2025 that some state bodies still access personal data outside the platform through COI technology, which qualifies the Government's statement that exchange takes place exclusively through MConnect but not the platform's use at scale.

The Agency was established by Government Decision No. 1028/2023 in December 2023 and launched in February 2024, and the Commission reports in 2026 that it occupies its offices with equipment installed and has been further strengthened. It was still recruiting in 2025, with 20 to 24 of about 45 posts filled, and the Commission finds that further efforts on operational capacity are needed, so there is no evidence yet of full operation at scale.

The ministry presented and published the White Paper in February 2024, but the Government itself describes it as declarative and not a policy document as such, and no source shows formal approval. The Commission reports that an AI and data sub-council applies its principles, and its recommendations were to be taken forward in a later national programme.

The new register was developed in 2024 but civil society monitoring covering January to November 2025 found it was not yet operational and data migration was incomplete, while the Government expected its launch at the end of 2025.

The Commission confirms that the State Register of Legal Units portal was launched on 29 December 2025 and that the system enables registration of all legal forms of entities. The Government describes a staged launch in pilot mode, with online applications for name reservation and register extracts available from February 2026, and no source yet gives evidence of use at scale.
Parliament adopted the Law on cybersecurity on 16 March 2023, with entry into force set for 1 January 2025, and the Commission found in 2023 that Moldova still needed to start implementing it.

The law has been in force since January 2025, and the Commission confirms that it empowers the Cybersecurity Agency to conduct audits. The Agency reports that it sent 307 notifications and issued 265 acts designating essential and important service providers in 2025, which is its own account and is not yet corroborated by an independent source.

Parliament adopted Law No. 195/2024 on 25 July 2024 to align with the GDPR, and it entered into force on 23 August 2026, as the Commission confirms. The sources describe preparation for its application, such as guidelines from the data protection authority, but none yet shows it being applied.
In 2025 the Commission found that Moldova lacked a comprehensive broadband mapping system, and the Government listed the mapping system and Single Information Point as actions still to be created.

The Commission reports in 2026 that the regulator operates a public broadband coverage platform, expanded since 2025, and has put into operation a Very High Capacity Networks map populated with data from the three mobile operators and the six largest fixed operators. No source shows the Single Information Point in operation, and in January 2026 the Government was still agreeing a joint action plan for the wider mapping system.

Law No. 200/2025 was adopted in July 2025 and, as the Commission confirms, entered into force in March 2026. The Commission notes that civil servant posts remain restricted to Moldovan nationals, and no source yet describes how the law is applied in practice.

SIGMA reports that the law obliges government agencies to exchange data only through the interoperability solution, and that the MConnect platform it governs is well functioning and used by many public and private organisations. The data protection authority finds that some state bodies still access data outside the platform in breach of the law, and the Government notes that replacing documents with data remains problematic in many cases.

The register was launched on 26 April 2023 and 67 authorities had registered 88 systems and 6 resources by the time of the Court of Accounts audit. The sources conflict on its coverage: SIGMA states that all state information resources and systems have been registered, while the Court of Accounts finds registration delayed, with 63% of registered systems not properly documented and some entries out of date.

Parliament approved the Law on electronic identification and trust services on 19 May 2022, and the Commission found it broadly but only partially aligned with the eIDAS Regulation. The sources give different dates for its entry into force, the Commission 10 December 2022 and the Government 1 January 2025, but agree it is in force; no source describes its application beyond its use as a reference for electronic submissions.

The Commission confirms that the National Council for Digital Transformation was established in November 2023 to coordinate the Digital Transformation Strategy, and it held its first meeting on 11 December 2023. The Commission also reports a sub-council on AI and data set up within it, but no source assesses how well the Council coordinates implementation.

The Ministry of Justice consulted publicly on the draft law in May 2025, and the data protection authority reported that in early 2026 it was still to undergo further consultation before submission to Parliament.

The Commission reports that Moldova adopted the law on the protection of personal data processed for crime prevention in August 2026, aligning with the Law Enforcement Directive. This rests on a single Commission statement, and no source yet describes its application.

The Commission confirms that Government Decision No. 222/2026 of 1 May 2026 set the legal framework for the Customs Decisions System, that 8 of 17 modules were in place by January 2026, after operators could first submit applications digitally from December 2024, and that by June 2026 all 17 types of applications and authorisations could be submitted and processed electronically. No source yet gives evidence of the volume of use.

SIGMA reported in 2023 that electronic signatures are available through MSign with about 200,000 active users, mostly businesses required to sign documents for the tax service. Government figures give more than 37 million documents signed through MSign in 2023 and more than 38 million in the first nine months of 2024.

The Commission confirms that the Government approved an SME digital transformation programme in 2022 alongside other SME support programmes, and the World Bank reports that the ministry and the SME agency created programmes to help businesses go digital. No source gives the number of enterprises supported or the results.

The Commission found no progress on the European Health Insurance Card in 2025, and in 2026 reports only that an EHIC Action Plan was approved as a roadmap for operational implementation. The legal amendments needed to introduce the card were planned for 2026 and no source shows them adopted or the card issued.

The concept note sets out a five-year programme to be approved by Government decision, with the ministry intending to draft and promote it in the second quarter of 2026. No source shows that the programme has been approved.

The Commission confirms that a Government decision of September 2025 designated the National Employment Agency as the EURES National Coordination Office, that an order of November 2025 set its tasks and the admission procedure for members, and that 10 territorial EURES members have been designated. A dedicated Labour Migration and EURES department has existed since January 2025, but the work so far is preparatory to joining EURES.

The ministry was developing the Public Sector e-Transformation Programme 2025-2030 in 2024 as one of three programmes under the Digital Transformation Strategy. No source shows that it has been approved.

The data protection authority reports that state bodies continue to access personal data in state registers through COI technology, with 13 entities still using it and only 5 having aligned their access over two years. The e-Governance Agency has asked authorities to end these contracts because COI does not meet security and traceability requirements, but no progress was recorded.

The Government set the organisation and operation of the Cybersecurity Coordinating Council by decision, and civil society monitoring describes it as tasked with coordinating cybersecurity policy and made up only of state institutions. No source describes its meetings or work.
In 2025 the Commission found Moldova well prepared to join the Common Transit Convention, with some technical arrangements pending, and set accession as a Reform Agenda step for December 2025.

The Commission reports that Moldova formally acceded to the Common Transit Convention in November 2025, after its New Computerised Transit System was connected to the common transit network. No source yet describes transit operations under the Convention.

The Commission confirms that the Information Technology and Cyber Security Service acts as the government's computer security incident response team. It had a staff of four in November 2022, and no source gives evidence of the incidents it handles.

The Court of Accounts treats the electronic register of employees as an information system developed and in use, owned by the Ministry of Finance since July 2022. It found that actions to interconnect it with other human resources systems were only partly implemented, without concrete results, and saw no evidence that data exchange with the health system was functional.

The employment agency reports 637,000 visits and 69,000 active users on angajat.md, and an international organisation describes the portal and mobile app as tools young people use to explore job opportunities. New modules, including vacancy import from external sources, were added in 2025.

Interoperability with the EU tax systems CESOP, OSS, VAT Refund, VAT REG and ViDA/VIES appears only as planned actions, and the Commission found in 2024 that Moldova had yet to familiarise itself with VIES. No source shows any of these connections in operation.
In 2025 joining the EU Third Countries Trusted List appeared as a planned step in the Reform Agenda and the Government's action plans.

The Commission reports that, following amendments to the law on electronic identification and trust services in December 2025, Moldova joined the EU third country trusted list for advanced electronic signatures and seals. The Government's own progress report records the data for inclusion as sent to the Commission.

The sources conflict: the Commission reports that amendments to the law on electronic identification and trust services in December 2025 fully aligned Moldova with EU digital identity requirements for qualified trust service providers, while the Government's progress report for 2025 states that the draft law is still being drafted. It is not clear whether the December 2025 amendments are this draft or a narrower change.

The Government proposes, in transposing the Digital Services Act, to designate the communications regulator as digital services coordinator and the Audiovisual Council as competent authority for video-sharing platforms. The Commission reports in 2026 only initial steps to set up the institutional framework, and no source shows the designation made.

The One-Stop Shop for documenting foreigners was set up under Government Decision No. 1187/2010 and is retained in the new rules on admitting foreigners, which allow applications there or electronically. Research finds that employers recruiting foreign workers must still gather several documents, so the bureaucratic procedure is not avoided, and no source gives figures on its use.

The employment agency reports that it continued to support displaced persons from Ukraine in 2024 and 2025, including visits to placement centres, and that 450 displaced jobseekers registered and 164 found work from January to September 2025. These are the agency's own figures, not corroborated by an independent or Commission source.

Civil society monitoring, citing the service's data, reports 129,384 active qualified electronic signature certificates in September 2022, of which 97,633 were USB tokens held by 45,870 unique users. The service is the only qualified trust service provider in Moldova and certificates are also issued through Public Services Agency offices.

Law No. 109/2025 on open data, partially transposing Directive (EU) 2019/1024, was adopted in May 2025 and followed by methodological norms in September 2025, according to the Government and civil society. The Commission dates the adoption of such a law to July 2026, which may refer to a later act; civil society reports training and platform improvements to apply it, but no source shows its effect on data publication.

The Commission described Moldova in 2023 as an active participant in TRACES NT with agreed harmonised certificates, but in 2026 it reports Moldova still preparing for full TRACES-NT integration, and the Government notes that full integration with EU systems such as TRACES remains to be aligned.

The Commission confirms that the e-Democracy platform was launched and has since been expanded with an e-Petitions module for consumer complaints, where individuals can submit petitions and track their status. No source gives figures on its use.

The Commission reports that Moldova harmonised its primary legislation with the European Electronic Communications Code and parts of the Roaming Regulation, and that secondary legislation including measures under the Code was also approximated. No source yet describes how the secondary rules are applied.

Government Decision No. 823/2025 approved the regulation on drafting, updating and implementing the National Response Plan for cyber incidents and crises, according to the Government and the Cybersecurity Agency. No source shows that the plan itself has been drawn up or approved.

The National Employment Agency provides employment, counselling and career guidance services, and Government figures show rising referrals for counselling. UNHCR finds that formal employment services such as the Agency remain underused, so the services operate but not at scale for the groups it examined.

The Competition Council is designated as the authority for Law No. 53/2025 on fairness and transparency for business users of online intermediation services. Its designation for the Digital Markets Act and a dedicated digital markets subdivision are still planned, and no source describes its supervisory work.

The regulator is to carry out a geographical survey of broadband coverage under Electronic Communications Law No. 72/2025, in force since 1 January 2026, with a legal deadline of 30 December 2030. No source shows the survey under way.

Government Decision No. 66/2026 established the Government Customer Support Service at the beginning of 2026, and the Government reports that the service was developed on time, with a pilot launch planned from January 2026. No source confirms that the pilot started or describes its use.

The Cybersecurity Agency reports that it held capture-the-flag and tabletop exercises in 2025 with public and private participants, jointly with Romanian and Ukrainian counterparts and EU mission experts. This is the Agency's own account and is not corroborated by an independent source.

The Commission confirms that Moldova signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, but civil society monitoring reports that it has not yet been ratified, and no source shows ratification.

The Commission reports that the social security agreement with Italy, signed in October 2024, entered into force in September 2025, and the social insurance house publishes the administrative arrangement and forms for Italy. No source gives evidence of how many claims have been handled under it.
The Reform Agenda sets a target of 18 of 19 taxpayer services digitalised by December 2026, with at least two in 2025 and two more in 2026. No source reports which services have been digitalised.
In 2025 the Commission recommended that Moldova ratify the second protocol to Convention 108, and the data protection authority repeated the recommendation.

The Commission reports that Moldova ratified the second Protocol of Council of Europe Convention 108 in May 2026. The sources do not make clear whether this is the same instrument as the amending Protocol CETS No. 223 recorded separately (INT-MDA-0608).

Moldova signed the Protocol amending Convention 108 in February 2023, and in early 2026 the draft ratification law was in interministerial consultation, with ratification planned to coincide with the entry into force of Law No. 195/2024 in August 2026. The Commission reports ratification of the second Protocol of Convention 108 in May 2026, recorded under INT-MDA-0609, but no source says whether that is this Protocol, so the analyst should decide whether the two entities should be merged.

The Commission confirms that the methodology on institutionalising life events for citizens and businesses was approved by Order No. 331 of the Secretary General of the Government on 18 December 2025. No source yet describes it being applied to services.

The Commission reports that a law amending several acts to set the legal basis for EU social security coordination rules and EESSI interconnection was adopted during its reporting period, after the draft was finalised in 2026. No source yet describes data exchange under it.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is part of the chapter and the only Chapter 2 sub-area wording among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files concerns legal alignment in general (2023) and the European Health Insurance Card (2025). The 2023 Analytical Report found no body responsible for enforcing the right to free movement of workers; Law No. 200/2025 gives the Equality Council that competence and the role of national contact point, as the Government reports in a machine-translated source, and the 2026 report confirms that the law entered into force in March 2026 to align with the acquis on workers' free movement rights. The improvement is legal only: the 2026 report does not assess the body, and the ten items of this run that name the Equality Council, all from the Government, concern its designation, staffing or planned measures, and none shows it at work for EU workers.

Law No. 200/2025 is adopted and designates the Equality Council, which answers the 2023 finding in law. The amendment of the Equality Council law, the Council's restructuring and extra staff, training for public authority and Council staff, and information measures by the General Inspectorate for Migration are all still planned, and the Council had filled 19 of 33 posts (Government figures, machine translated). What remains is a body that in practice supports EU workers and informs them of their rights, with the mandate, structure and staff to do so.

The missing enforcement body is raised only in the 2023 Analytical Report: a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no later EU item on the Equality Council or an enforcement body, and no benchmark, Reform Agenda payment condition or key recommendation naming it. It is a specific acquis obligation within the chapter but not central to it, and the 2026 key recommendations address alignment and equal treatment of EU workers in general terms.

The legal designation is done, and the remaining steps (amending the Equality Council law, restructuring and recruiting) are within the Government's control, with one lead body already in place. Staffing is the main constraint: the Council had 19 of 33 planned posts filled and its anti-discrimination directorate 4 of 7 (Government figures, machine translated).

Sub-area wording on the European Health Insurance Card, which matches this issue, records no progress in 2025, and the finding that no national health insurance card exists because there is no integrated health information system is unchanged in the 2023 report, the 2023 Analytical Report and the 2024 and 2025 reports. In 2026 the Commission reports a finalised feasibility study and an approved EHIC Action Plan, which are planning steps and do not yet show a change in the card or the health information system.

The 2025 and 2026 key recommendations still require IT infrastructure, systems and capacity for the EHIC scheme. Only the feasibility study is implemented: the EHIC module in the health insurance information system, the amendments to the health care and health insurance laws, the technical specifications of the card and the integrated health information system are planned or under development, and the Government states that the EU acts on the card are not yet transposed (machine translated). What remains is a national health insurance card and the IT, legal and administrative basis to issue and accept the European Health Insurance Card at accession.

The EHIC is named in the Chapter 2 key recommendations of 2025 and 2026, and the finding that its domestic preconditions are missing is repeated in each report from 2023 to 2025, with no progress recorded in 2025. Issuing and accepting the card is a core acquis requirement for accession, which is why the issue is rated High although the key recommendation itself appears in only two reports.

The national health insurance company coordinates the work, the feasibility study is finished, an action plan sets a roadmap and the law amendments are planned for 2026. Against that, the card depends on an integrated health information system that the Commission found missing in each report from 2023 to 2025, and the insurer's IT directorate had 3 of 8 planned specialists (machine translated).

This issue is not raised in EU material: a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no EU item on consulting the data protection authority on draft laws or on following its opinions, and the four items on the issue all date from 2026 (the data protection authority's 2025 activity report and its machine-translated opinion on a draft law). One year of evidence gives no sequence from which to read a direction.

This issue is not raised in EU material, so there is no EU requirement to compare against. The authority's own report shows that it reviewed 208 draft acts in 2025 and asked for changes to most of them, but a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no item showing whether its advice on draft acts was then followed. What remains is to establish whether the authority's opinions are taken into account.

This issue is not raised in EU material, as a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no EU item on it, which keeps its priority from being High, and its four items come only from the data protection authority. Consultation of the authority is a procedural matter at the edge of the data protection theme.

Consulting the authority and acting on its opinions is a procedural step within the control of the Government and Parliament, and the authority already reviews a large number of drafts. Apart from the authority's account of years of unheeded requests to stop access to state registers outside the interoperability platform, a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no item showing past progress or resistance on the uptake of its opinions on draft acts, so the rating rests mainly on the nature of the mechanism.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this issue concerns only part of Chapter 23. The 2024 report says justice digitalisation needs to improve, the 2025 report that the new Agency for Digitalisation in Justice needs faster operationalisation, and the 2026 report finds the Agency's capacity extremely limited and the use of IT tools across the justice system uneven and partial. The August 2026 amendments promoting digitalisation of some judicial procedures are recorded but not yet assessed.

The 2026 report calls for further legal improvements and a decisive strengthening of the Agency, and a 2026 key recommendation asks for substantial progress on an integrated electronic case management system for law enforcement and prosecution bodies. The Agency exists but has extremely limited capacity, the August 2026 amendments are adopted, and the E-File application, which the Reform Agenda requires in all first instance courts by December 2027, is still planned. What remains is digital communication with courts in practice and connected IT across justice institutions, run by an agency able to deliver it.

Digital case filing in courts is a Reform Agenda payment condition (E-File in all first instance courts by December 2027), an integrated case management system for law enforcement and prosecution is a 2026 key recommendation, and justice digitalisation is raised in each report from 2024 to 2026. Both requirements are open and central to digital justice.

Progress needs courts, prosecution and law enforcement bodies to adopt connected systems, and the agency set up to deliver this has extremely limited capacity because of persistent staffing problems in 2026. Past progress is limited to setting up the agency in 2025 and the August 2026 amendments, and IT use remains uneven.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only, since this is part of the chapter: some level of preparation from 2023 to 2025 and moderately prepared in 2026. The 2026 report finds that the new legal framework reinforced the regulator's administrative and financial independence, and the Commission's 2026 release decision records access tariffs for the incumbent's infrastructure cut by 16% to 49% from 1 March 2026, against minimal network sharing (0.95%) in the 2025 baseline. The gain on independence is legal only, and an ITU finding reported in the Government's 2025 programme still describes independence and accountability as insufficient (machine translated).

The Reform Agenda requires at least 3% of the incumbent's infrastructure to be shared and network-sharing agreements by the incumbent; access tariffs have been cut and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act transposed in June 2026, but the agreements are still planned and no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files reports the sharing rate after the 0.95% baseline. The law reinforcing the regulator's independence is adopted, and the regulator had filled 105 of 114 posts by March 2026. What remains is independence shown in practice and competitive safeguards that actually raise infrastructure sharing in a market where the incumbent holds more than half of broadband.

The Reform Agenda conditions on infrastructure sharing touch the competition side of this issue, but they are framed as implementing the Electronic Communications Code and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act, whose alignment belongs to the legal alignment issue. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found regulator independence in no benchmark, key recommendation or Reform Agenda payment condition; the Commission mentions it only in its 2026 finding that the new law reinforced it.

The levers are legal and regulatory and within national control, and recent delivery is strong: a new law in force from January 2026, updated access tariffs in force within the Reform Agenda timetable, working arrangements with BEREC from 2025 and a regulator close to full staffing. The main constraint is market concentration, with the incumbent holding more than half of broadband.

The Chapter 6 scale is context only, since this is part of the chapter. The 2023 report and the 2023 Analytical Report found company law not aligned on digital tools and processes, the 2024 report repeated the recommendation while recording a qualified electronic signature for filing with the business register, and the 2026 report records the new State Register of Legal Entities, launched in December 2025, which enables registration of all legal forms. The Government's own assessment (machine translated) is that the directive on digital tools in company law is only partly transposed.

The latest EU requirement, from 2024, is further alignment on the use of digital tools and processes in company law. Electronic signature filing and the new register are implemented, but the draft law on digital tools in company law is still planned, online company registration ran by e-mail as a provisional solution, and in February 2026 the new platform offered online only name reservation and register extracts (machine translated). What remains is full transposition of the rules on digital tools and processes, with company formation and filings fully online through the new register.

Digital tools in company law appear in the 2023 recommendation and among many elements of the 2024 key recommendation on company law, but a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found them in no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition and in no 2025 or 2026 item repeating the recommendation. It is a defined acquis requirement but a narrow part of Chapter 6; the Reform Agenda step on the new register is counted under the base registers issue.

The remaining work is mainly legal and within the Government's control: a draft law on digital tools in company law is planned and the new register is in place. Against that, the register slipped from a planned July 2025 launch to December 2025 and online company registration still ran by e-mail as a provisional solution, so delays are the main risk (Government figures, machine translated).

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is a cross-cutting data protection issue. Breaches are confirmed every year: 105 in 2022 in the 2023 report and 173 violations, given by CSO Meter for 2024 and by the authority's 2025 activity report for 2025, which may be one count reported for two different years; the 2025 report records a major health data breach, and the authority reports in 2026 that state bodies still access personal data through the COI technology. Rising complaints are read by CSO Meter as growing awareness rather than worse compliance, so they are not used as a trend.

The 2023 requirement to train public servants and raise awareness has been answered by the authority's 2025 training campaign of 84 courses for over 3,600 people, and Law No. 195/2024, adopted and in force from 23 August 2026, lets the authority impose administrative sanctions directly. Sources conflict on data access: the Government says, in a machine-translated source, that data exchange takes place exclusively through MConnect, while the authority finds state bodies still using the COI technology outside it, and only about 50 public authorities had designated a data protection officer. What remains is compliance in practice by public and private controllers, including in health, with the new sanctions applied and access to state registers made traceable.

Data protection compliance is raised in the 2023 recommendation on training and awareness and in the 2025 key recommendation on health, which names the protection of personal data, but a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found it in no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition, and not across three or more reports. Applying data protection law is central to the data theme, but the volume of authority and civil society material does not raise priority.

The new law gives the authority direct administrative sanctions, ending the duplicated procedures it blames for weak deterrence, and courts upheld its measures in 52 of 58 final cases in 2025. Against that, compliance depends on many public and private controllers, and the authority reports years of unanswered requests to move state bodies off the COI technology.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is a cross-cutting e-government issue. The Commission found the civil service human resources information system not functional in 2023 and 2024, its replacement only in incipient design in 2025 and still in development in 2026. Shared platforms such as MCloud, MPass, MPay and MConnect were already in place before the period, as the Reform Agenda notes, so they show no change.

Most shared building blocks are implemented and in use, but the human resources management system, which the Reform Agenda requires with at least three modules by December 2027, is still in development, the permits system was used fully or partly by only 16 of 31 issuing institutions at the 2024 audit, and the eArhiva system is planned. Sources conflict on the register of state information systems: SIGMA says all resources and systems were registered, while the Court of Accounts finds registration delayed. What remains is a working human resources management system and consistent use of shared systems by all institutions, including those not subordinate to the Government.

The human resources management system is a Reform Agenda payment condition and is reported in each year from 2023 to 2026, but it mainly serves civil service management rather than shared e-government services, and the Commission records the shared platforms as in place.

Moldova has a long record of building shared platforms through the e-Governance Agency, and the human resources system has a Reform Agenda deadline. Against that, the earlier system failed through problems with its private provider, its replacement has moved slowly since 2023, and institutions not subordinate to the Government declined to use the permits system (machine translated).

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this issue spans several chapters; the 2026 Chapter 6 rating of some progress cites the new register and is context only. The Commission recorded the business register's paper archive digitalised by August 2024 and the State Register of Legal Units launched on 29 December 2025, a Reform Agenda step it judged satisfactorily fulfilled, while the public property register was in progress in 2025 and still pending in 2026. The State Population Register concept was withdrawn in August 2025 and resumed in 2026 (machine translated), so not every register moved.

The 2025 and 2026 key recommendations require completing the digitalisation of the public property register, which remains in progress, and the Reform Agenda requires a digital cadastre covering 98% of the territory by December 2027; the legal entities register is implemented. Sources conflict on the register of state information systems: SIGMA says all were registered, while the Court of Accounts finds registration delayed and 63% of registered systems not properly documented. What remains is a fully digital public property register, the planned modernisation of the population register and the cadastre, and reliable data across base registers.

Base registers are named in two Reform Agenda payment conditions (the State Register of Legal Units and the digital cadastre), and the public property register is a key recommendation in 2025 and 2026; reliable base registers are central to the data and digital government themes. The legal entities register condition is already met, so the rating rests mainly on the cadastre condition and the repeated recommendation.

The legal entities register was delivered with World Bank support, about six months after its planned July 2025 launch, and the civil status records system went into production in November 2025. Against that, the population register concept was suspended in 2025, the public property register has been in progress since 2025, and the Commission found the Public Services Agency short of administrative capacity in 2024.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only, though its progress wording cites the digitalisation of public services in 2024 and progress on all key performance indicators in 2025. Commission figures are about 40% in both 2023 (business services online) and 2024 (mapped services) and rise from then on, on differing measures: over 50% in 2025 (64% for businesses and 54% for individuals in 2024), and in 2026 70.3% of the 636 services on the EVO portal online, 82% of business and 61% of citizen services digitalised and user uptake up significantly. Government counts of 2023 business service requests conflict between its 2024 and 2025 documents, so they are not used for the trend.

The Reform Agenda target of 75% of business services digitalised has been met, and EVO, the public services portal and 118 Unified Public Service Centres are in use; but in 2026 only 61% of citizen services are digitalised, only 133 of 414 business services run fully end to end, the Reform Agenda notes that the portal lacks integration with EU systems, and the link to the Single Digital Gateway is still planned. Demand remains low in rural areas, which is why the Commission says the centres were set up. What remains is a fuller range of citizen services delivered end to end online, integration with EU systems, and use by people with weaker digital access or skills.

Digital public services are the subject of two Reform Agenda payment conditions: the EVO Sign wallet integrating at least 20 e-services by December 2026, which is still open and shared with the electronic identification issue, and 75% of business services digitalised, which the Commission found met in 2026. The Commission's 2024 Chapter 10 progress wording cites notable progress on digitalising public services, and the portal and its services are central to the digital government theme, so the rating rests on the open wallet condition rather than on the fulfilled step.

Progress has been steady and measured by the Commission in every report from 2023 to 2026, the e-Governance Agency runs the shared platforms, and the work is tied to Reform Agenda funding. The main constraints are cost, which the Government says exceeds its own resources, and low demand among older and rural users.

The Commission found that EU citizens had no access to posts in public administration bodies in the 2023 report and the 2023 analytical report, and repeated the finding unchanged in the 2024 and 2025 reports. The 2026 report records that new legislation opened certain technical, specialised and auxiliary posts to EU citizens while civil servant posts remain reserved to nationals, so the improvement is legal only and partial.

Government Decision No. 566/2025 opens technical, specialist and auxiliary posts to persons without Moldovan citizenship, which the Commission confirms in 2026, and the Government plans an analysis, in the light of case law of the Court of Justice, of which civil service functions can be opened; its own account still excludes public functions that expressly require citizenship. What remains is opening civil servant posts to EU citizens, except those that involve the exercise of public authority and safeguarding the general interests of the State.

The finding is repeated in the 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports and concerns a core rule of the chapter, but it sits in the body text: a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on public sector posts. Partial legal progress is recorded in 2026, so the route to High for a core requirement with no progress does not apply.

The change is a national legal matter with no dependence on other states, and the 2025 Government decision shows that categories of posts can be opened. The remaining step needs a review of civil service functions against case law, which the Government has so far only planned.

The 2023 analytical report found that national law covers most branches of social security but not pre-retirement benefits, gives no unemployment benefit to non-nationals with temporary residence, and needs capacity building in coordination; a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no Commission item on this alignment in the 2024 or 2025 reports, so the wording is not repeated across three reports and the default of persistent does not apply. The 2026 report records the adoption of a law setting a legal basis for applying the coordination rules, which is improvement in law only: the Commission does not assess its alignment and asks for gap analyses of the coordination regulations, and the 2023 gap on unemployment benefit remains open. The Chapter 2 rating rose from an early stage in 2023 and 2024 to between some and a moderate level of preparation in 2026, but the progress it cites concerns bilateral agreements and EURES, so the scale was not decisive.

A law establishing the legal basis for applying the EU coordination rules and EESSI interconnection has been adopted, which is a legal step only, while the draft law on keeping unemployment benefit when moving and on frontier workers remains a proposal, and the Government states that current law does not regulate these cases; only 3 of 8 planned staff of the legal directorate work on harmonisation with European rules. What remains is a gap analysis and full alignment of national pension, health, unemployment and other social security law with Regulations (EC) No 883/2004 and No 987/2009, together with the administrative measures to apply them at accession.

Alignment with the coordination regulations is core acquis for the chapter, and the 2026 key recommendation asks for gap analyses of them. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found the requirement only in the 2023 analytical report and the 2026 report, not in a key recommendation repeated across three reports, a benchmark or a Reform Agenda payment condition.

The legal changes are within national control: a coordination law has been adopted and a detailed draft on unemployment benefits prepared. Against that, the work spans several institutions and benefit systems, specialist staff are few and the draft ties key provisions to the date of accession.

The 2023 analytical report found that authorities struggle with administrative capacity and data exchange in international cases, and the 2025 key recommendation asked Moldova to develop IT infrastructure for EESSI. In 2026 the Commission reports that the e-Governance Agency was designated as the EESSI National Access Point with two liaison bodies, a law setting the basis for EESSI interconnection was adopted and an EESSI Action Plan approved, while the 2026 key recommendation still asks for the IT infrastructure and capacity. The improvement is organisational and legal only, as no technical connection is reported.

The access point, liaison bodies, legal basis and action plan are in place, but the Government reports that the employment agency and CNAS systems still need adjusting for EESSI, that the technical solution and its financing will be chosen later, and that only 3 of 8 planned IT directorate staff work on the health insurance card and interconnection with European systems. What remains is the IT infrastructure, interconnected information systems, staff and funding for full participation in EESSI and for electronic exchange of health insurance data.

Electronic exchange is needed to apply social security coordination at accession, and it is named in the key recommendations of the 2025 and 2026 reports. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found EESSI in five Commission items, all from 2025 and 2026, and in no key recommendation repeated across three reports, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition.

The 2026 designations and action plan show that organisational steps can be taken, and the Government reports the interoperability platform as technically ready for cross-border exchange. Connection, however, depends on technical documentation from the Commission, an investment not yet decided, several institutions and a new employment agency system funded externally.

The issue is not raised in EU material: a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files for corruption prevention, integrity or internal audit in the bodies administering worker mobility found one item, the employment agency's own report of internal audit missions, one of them on how the EURES network is being implemented. A single item gives no sequence over time.

No EU item states a requirement on corruption prevention in the administration of worker mobility: the only Moldova item on this issue, found by a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, is the employment agency's own report of internal audit missions, which says nothing on integrity policy or internal controls. What remains is unknown, since no source states a requirement or a problem for Moldova on this issue.

The only Moldova item on this issue, found by a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, is the employment agency's own report, not an EU source, so priority cannot be High. The item reports audit activity and does not describe a problem.

The one item shows that the employment agency has an internal audit service that carried out five assurance missions, but it gives no evidence on the actors, mechanisms or past progress needed to judge how tractable corruption prevention is.

The issue is not raised in EU material: a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files for host-language or Romanian-language tuition found eight items, none from an EU source, and the 2026 report says only that the free movement law aims to align with the acquis on the education of migrant workers' children, with no finding on tuition. The issue first appears in the Government's 2025 accession programme, which plans Romanian courses for EU citizens, their family members and their children, so there is no earlier item from which to judge a trend.

All the measures are proposals: Romanian courses in schools and through the national programme for learning Romanian, a new programme for 2026 to 2028 with study centres, and a mechanism to pay teachers, and the Government says these could need additional teaching posts. What remains is, on the Government's own account, putting in place and resourcing host-language tuition for EU workers, their family members and their children.

The issue is not raised in EU material: a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files for host-language or Romanian-language tuition found no EU item on it, which keeps priority from being High, and it rests on the Government's 2025 accession programme, which describes planned measures. Host-language tuition is a narrow strand of the chapter compared with access to employment and social security coordination.

Delivery rests mainly with the Ministry of Education and Research and builds on an existing national programme for learning Romanian. However, the new programme was still to be drafted in 2025, and no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files reports funding for the planned teacher payment mechanism or for extra teaching posts.

The 2023 key recommendation asked Moldova to adopt the Digital Transformation Strategy 2023-2030 and ensure capacity to implement it; the strategy was adopted in September 2023 and a National Council for Digital Transformation set up in November 2023, as the 2024 report records. The 2025 report notes an implementation programme for 2025 to 2027 and tangible progress on all key performance indicators, and the 2026 report again records progress on them. The Chapter 10 rating rose from some level of preparation in 2023 to 2025 to moderately prepared in 2026, but it rates the whole chapter and was not decisive.

The strategy, the council and an implementation programme are in place, but the Commission repeats in 2024, 2025 and 2026 its key recommendation to ensure institutional capacity to implement the strategy. The Government reports 225 million lei of the programme's cost as uncovered, the ministry and the e-Governance Agency responsible for 53 and 37 of its 68 actions, and a lack of centralised coordination, and a 2024 follow-up audit by the Court of Accounts found its recommendation on documenting information systems only partly implemented, citing insufficient institutional capacity. What remains is the staff, funding and coordination capacity in the ministry and the e-Governance Agency to deliver and monitor the strategy.

A key recommendation on adopting the strategy and ensuring the institutional capacity to implement it appears in the 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, and strategy and governance are central to the digital transformation theme. The later recommendations name data protection and cybersecurity as the main areas for that capacity, which are covered by other issues.

The Government adopted the strategy, set up the council and approved the implementation programme within two years, and the Commission records progress on its indicators. Capacity is the harder part: the Government and the Court of Accounts report staff shortages, low pay for IT staff, staff turnover after reorganisations and reliance on external partners for funding.

The 2023 and 2024 reports find that the tax administration improved its electronic services, and the 2025 and 2026 reports record good progress in Chapter 16 that includes the digitalisation of tax administration services. The 2026 report still finds it essential to digitalise tax services further. The Chapter 16 statements cover the whole chapter, so the issue's own items were decisive.

The Reform Agenda sets a target of 18 of 19 taxpayer services digitalised by December 2026 and the 2026 report asks for further digitalisation, while the Government's indicator gives 64% of companies using e-invoices against a target above 70%. SIGMA found that only 10% of citizens filed personal income tax returns electronically for 2022, and the Reform Agenda names limited staff and taxpayers' preference for in-person services as barriers. What remains is completing the digitalisation of taxpayer services and raising their use, especially by citizens.

The digitalisation of taxpayer services is a Reform Agenda payment condition due by December 2026 and is repeated in the 2026 report, but it is a narrow strand of digital government on which the Commission records good progress in 2025 and 2026. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no key recommendation naming taxpayer e-services; the 2026 key recommendation on the tax administration concerns the State Tax Service's digital transformation programme and compliance risk management.

The work lies with one agency, the Reform Agenda sets yearly targets with payments attached, and the Commission records improvement in every report from 2023 to 2026. Uptake depends partly on taxpayers' habits, which the Reform Agenda names as a barrier.

The 2023 report found limited progress on an e-health legal framework and no e-health strategy, and the 2024 report found no integrated health information system, although electronic prescriptions had operated since April 2024. The Reform Agenda in 2025 still notes no approved eHealth strategy or regulatory framework, and the 2026 report records the adoption of the National Programme for Digitalisation and Innovation in Health 2025-2030 and a modernised ePrescription system with fully digital certificates. The improvement is in strategy and in one service, as the integrated system and electronic health records are not yet in place.

A health digitalisation programme is adopted and ePrescription works, but the legal framework, the electronic health record and the national e-health entity are still planned, with the record due for 40% of the insured population by December 2027. The Government itself names the lack of a functional electronic health record, limited interoperability and no dedicated institutional framework as major challenges. What remains is a legal framework on eHealth aligned with the EU acquis, an interoperable integrated health information system and electronic health records in use.

Electronic health records for 40% of the insured population by December 2027 are an open Reform Agenda payment condition, and the key recommendations on health in the 2024 and 2025 reports name an integrated e-health system, interoperability and the digitalisation of health services. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no 2026 recommendation on e-health, so the rating rests on the open payment condition together with the two key recommendations; eHealth is a major digital public service within the theme.

The Government has adopted a programme and runs an ePrescription system that the Commission reports as modernised, which shows delivery capacity. The health record and interoperability need new legislation, a new institution, several health bodies and substantial funding in the Government's own estimates.

The 2022 Opinion found limited alignment with the EU electronic communications framework, and the 2023 report asked for alignment with the Electronic Communications Code and the Roaming Regulation. The 2024 report found that alignment had started and the 2025 report noted legislative advancements; in 2026 the Commission found the roaming acquis correctly transposed in full, the Code transposed in primary law with secondary legislation approximated, and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act reflected in a law adopted in June 2026. The Chapter 10 rating rates the whole chapter and was not decisive.

Law No. 72/2025, in force since January 2026, the roaming law and its secondary acts, and the 2026 infrastructure law respond to the requirements, and the Commission judged the related Reform Agenda step satisfactorily fulfilled. The regulator is still drafting secondary acts under the new law, an end-user protection regulation is planned for 2026, the Government plans to transpose the remaining electronic communications acts by the end of 2027, and a civil society monitor describes the new law as only partly compatible with the Code. What remains is completing and applying the secondary legislation under the Code and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act and transposing the remaining related acts.

Alignment with the roaming acquis and the Code was a key recommendation in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports and part of a Reform Agenda step, which would usually mean High. The Commission now finds the roaming acquis fully transposed and the step fulfilled, and a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no recommendation on electronic communications or roaming in the 2026 report, so the remaining work is narrower.

The main laws were adopted in 2025 and 2026 with EU technical support, and the Commission confirms the results, including entry into Roam Like at Home in January 2026. The remaining work is secondary legislation by one regulator and one ministry, which the regulator is already drafting.

The 2023 and 2024 reports call for more investment in infrastructure, including to overcome the rural-urban digital divide, and the 2025 Reform Agenda notes the absence of a comprehensive broadband mapping system. In 2026 the Commission found that the regulator's coverage platform and a new map of very high capacity networks provide relevant monitoring for investment decisions, while the 2026 report says that infrastructure investment remains well below needs. The issue spans several chapters, so chapter ratings were not decisive.

The mapping system is in operation, but the geographical survey of broadband coverage has a legal deadline of December 2030, the development of networks in white areas waits for it, and the state aid rules for broadband exist only as a draft. What remains is a national investment framework, with state aid rules and funding, that brings broadband to rural and white areas in line with EU connectivity targets.

The broadband mapping system was a Reform Agenda step, now fulfilled, and the 2023 and 2024 key recommendations on competitiveness ask for infrastructure investment, but they name digital infrastructure alongside energy and transport. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no key recommendation specific to broadband planning.

The mapping step was delivered by 2026 through data sharing among the regulator, the cadastre agency and operators, and a World Bank project is analysing financing models. Extending networks to small and isolated localities needs substantial investment, and the Government's own timetable for the coverage survey runs to 2030.

The 2023 and 2024 reports found Moldova not aligned with the acquis on geo-blocking, platform-to-business relations, the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act, and the 2025 report still found no alignment on the first two and the Digital Markets Act while noting that work on the Digital Services Act had started. The 2026 report finds alignment on geo-blocking and platform-to-business relations partial, with additional legislation in force in 2026, and initial steps on the institutional framework for both Acts. The improvement is legal and partial only.

Two 2025 laws partly transpose the platform-to-business and geo-blocking regulations, although Government sources give conflicting law numbers for them, the Competition Council is designated for the first, and the e-Commerce Directive is broadly aligned. The digital services law is still being drafted, the Digital Markets Act mechanism needs an amendment to the competition law, no supervisory authority for digital services exists yet, and the Government notes missing enforcement rules under the platform-to-business regulation. What remains is a legal basis and enforcement capacity for the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act, and full alignment on geo-blocking and platform-to-business relations.

The 2024 and 2025 key recommendations ask Moldova to adopt and implement digital services legislation, bundled with media legislation, and the 2026 report repeats the need in its body text on binding acquis. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found it in no key recommendation in three reports, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition.

Two laws were adopted in 2025, and the Government plans to align with the Digital Services Act by the end of 2026, with EU4Digital experts helping on the draft. Enforcement needs new units in two regulators, while the ministry has one post for this area.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is only part of the chapter and the only Chapter 2 sub-area wording among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files concerns legal alignment in general (2023) and the European Health Insurance Card (2025). A search of all items for the European Labour Authority and Regulation (EU) 2019/1149 found the Commission's two records of the May 2025 cooperation agreement and Government items on the agreement and a draft law; none is a finding or recommendation on alignment, so there is no sequence from which to read a direction.

The Commission records that Moldova signed a cooperation agreement with the European Labour Authority in May 2025, which covers the arrangements for cooperating with it. The government states that the draft law to harmonise national legislation with Regulation (EU) 2019/1149 is still being prepared, and gives this only as its own account. What remains is adopting and applying the law that aligns national legislation with the regulation, including the Authority's role as mediator, and building the capacity of the ministry, the employment agency and the labour inspectorate to cooperate with it.

A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no Commission requirement, key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on the European Labour Authority; the Commission mentions it only to record the 2025 cooperation agreement. Cooperation with the Authority is a small part of the chapter.

The change is narrow, legal and within the control of the labour ministry, and the cooperation agreement was concluded in 2025, which shows recent progress with the Authority. A draft law has already been identified, although its adoption date is not given.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is only part of the chapter and the only Chapter 2 sub-area wording among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files concerns legal alignment in general (2023) and the European Health Insurance Card (2025). The 2023 report, the 2023 Analytical Report and the 2024 report all find that EU rules on supplementary pension rights of mobile workers are not incorporated into Moldovan law and that there is no occupational pension scheme, and in 2025 the government still describes the occupational system as at an early stage and plans full transposition of Directive 98/49/EC.

Sources conflict: the Commission in 2024 says the EU rules are not incorporated into Moldovan law, while the government in 2025 says, on the basis of the financial market regulator's conformity tables, that the law is aligned with Directive 2014/50/EU and partly transposes Directive 98/49/EC. The responses named by the government, full transposition of Directive 98/49/EC and a draft amendment to Law No. 198/2020, are not yet adopted. What remains is incorporating the EU rules on acquiring and preserving supplementary pension rights into Moldovan law in a form the Commission accepts.

The finding is repeated in the 2023 and 2024 reports, but a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on supplementary pension rights. Moldova has no occupational pension scheme, so the rules have limited practical reach, and the issue is a small part of the chapter.

The change is legal and lies with the government and the financial market regulator, and a draft amendment to the voluntary pension funds law is identified. Against that, the government and the Commission disagree on how far the law is already aligned, and no adoption date is given for the draft.

The chapter scale was used as context only, since this is part of the chapter; the issue's own items show change. The 2023 report and Analytical Report and the 2024 report find that no authority is responsible for open data policies, and the 2025 report finds Moldova not yet aligned with the Open Data Directive; the 2026 report records a law partially harmonising with that Directive, and the government reports a dedicated open data unit created in the economy ministry under Law No. 109/2025. The improvement is legal and institutional only: across all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files the only measure of publication is the Government's count of 1,268 datasets on the portal, a single figure with no trend, and the World Bank found the portal still lacking in use in 2024.

The law on open data and re-use, its methodological rules and a two-person policy unit address the Commission's findings on alignment and on the absence of a responsible authority, but the law only partly transposes the Directive. The government itself says the data.gov.md portal needs updating and completing with data, the World Bank finds the portal still lacking in use, and the draft law on data governance has been suspended until 2027. What remains is full alignment with the Open Data Directive and related EU data rules, and regular publication and updating of datasets by institutions on the portal.

The Commission repeats the finding on open data in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and the 2024 Growth Plan Communication refers to implementing the Open Data Directive, but a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on open data. Open data is a defined part of the data theme rather than its centre.

Recent legal progress is recorded, with a law, methodological rules and a responsible unit in place, and the portal already exists. Against that, capacity is thin, with two posts in the ministry and one at the e-Governance Agency for the portal, and publication depends on many institutions, including local authorities, whose capacity the government lists as a challenge.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is only part of the chapter. The 2023 report finds 39 staff for 45 posts with high turnover, the 2024 and 2025 reports call for more capacity, especially staff, and the 2026 report says the authority's human, technical and financial capacities have not grown with its expanded mandate. The authority's own 2025 report gives 36 staff at the end of 2025 and a turnover rate of 18%, which confirms the finding but is its own account.

The Commission's latest finding is that capacities remain limited while Law No. 195/2024 has widened the mandate, and the response aimed at capacity, strengthening the authority's administrative and human resources, has not yet been carried out. The authority itself reports pay below comparable supervisory bodies, staff overload and pressure on staff, and gives this as its own account. What remains is giving the National Centre for Personal Data Protection the staff, pay, budget and safeguards it needs to supervise independently under the new law.

An adequately resourced and independent supervisory authority is a core requirement of the EU data protection acquis, and the Commission records the shortfall in the 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports with no increase in capacity recorded, which meets the test for High without a benchmark. The 2025 Enlargement Communication's call for more resources and independence for data protection authorities applies to all enlargement countries and only supports this.

The remedy is within the government's control, through the staffing limit, pay and budget, and Law No. 195/2024 was adopted. Against that, staff numbers fell from 39 in the 2023 report to 36 at the end of 2025 despite repeated recommendations, and the authority links turnover to pay below comparable bodies, which needs wider pay decisions.

The chapter scale was used as context only, since this is part of the chapter. The 2023 report asks Moldova to join the third-country trusted list and the 2024 report asks for interoperability with European Digital Identity Wallets; the 2026 report records amendments in December 2025 that fully align the rules for qualified trust service providers, joining the trusted list and cross-border testing of the national wallet. Use has not changed in the same way: the Commission gives 200 000 users, 9.8% of adults, in 2024 and over 266 000, 10% of adults, in 2025.

Recognition has advanced through the December 2025 amendments, the trusted list and new identity cards carrying a qualified signature, but the Reform Agenda condition for December 2026 also requires an EU-aligned national wallet integrating at least 20 e-services, and the wallet was only started in September 2025, with remote identification moved to 2027. Use remains low, with about 10% of the population holding qualified certificates and fees of at least 11 euros a year reported by civil society in 2026. What remains is a working EU-aligned wallet, mutual recognition in practice and much wider, cheaper use of electronic identification and signatures.

The national wallet aligned with EU standards, joining the third-country trusted list and alignment with eIDAS 2 are a Reform Agenda payment condition due in December 2026, and the Commission raised the trusted list and wallet interoperability in the 2023 and 2024 reports. Electronic identification is the centre of this theme.

Legal and recognition steps have moved quickly, with Law No. 117/2025, the December 2025 amendments and the trusted list, and the work lies mainly with the e-Governance Agency and the trust service provider. Against that, use has stayed near 10% of adults, the eKYC deadline has slipped to 2027, and within the 2025 consultation another government body described EVOSign as still at the pilot stage and not ready for use in systems.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since the issue comes from a cross-cutting theme. In 2023 the Commission finds no electronic biometric database and asks for planning towards Eurodac, and in 2026 it finds security and data protection weaknesses in the border police system and asks for interoperability ahead of a future connection to EU large-scale systems; a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no item from the 2024 or 2025 reports on Eurodac, VIS, ECRIS or other EU large-scale systems. Wider use of SIENA, which the 2026 report records, is the one change, and it concerns Europol's exchange channel rather than the EU systems in this issue.

Apart from SIENA, the responses to the latest requirements are plans: interoperability of the fingerprint register with Eurodac, a national visa system interoperable with VIS, an analysis, by the end of 2027, of how to make the criminal records register interoperable with ECRIS and ECRIS-TCN, and a joint study with eu-LISA. The government reports a partial transposition of the Eurodac regulation in the fingerprint law, which is legal only. What remains is building or upgrading the migration, border and justice systems so that they are secure and ready to connect to Eurodac, VIS, ECRIS and the other EU large-scale systems.

The Commission repeats the call for data exchange through SIENA in the 2023 and 2026 key recommendations and raises Eurodac and EU large-scale systems in 2023 and 2026, but connection to most of these systems is expected only towards accession and a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on these systems.

There is evidence of progress on SIENA, rolled out to several law enforcement bodies, and the government has a plan covering each system. Against that, the work needs the interior ministry, the migration inspectorate, the border police, justice bodies and eu-LISA, and the systems for Eurodac and VIS are still to be built or upgraded.

The chapter scales were not decisive, since this issue spans several chapters and is part of each. The main thread is taxation: the Commission finds no IT strategy for interoperability with EU tax systems in 2023 and 2024, records a programme prepared in 2025, and in 2026 records a roadmap for 2026 to 2029 while finding that EMCS and SEED solutions remain to be developed and that VIES interoperability must advance. The plans are adopted but no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files records a new connection to an EU tax or excise system, and the 2026 report adds that Moldova is not yet in ECURIE or EURDEP.

Some connections exist, such as access to TED since 2020, trademark data in EUIPO systems and use of TRACES, but they lie outside the latest requirements. The responses to those requirements are a tax IT programme and roadmap that are adopted, and connections to the CCN gateway, VIES and other tax systems, TESTA and IMI that are planned.
