What remains is building and connecting the tax, excise, radiological, civil protection and internal market systems to the EU systems the Commission names.

Tax interoperability is a core acquis requirement raised in the 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, but the Commission records good progress in the taxation chapter in 2025 and 2026, so the test for High on lack of progress is not met. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on it: the Reform Agenda's tax objective refers to EU taxation IT systems, but its step concerns taxpayer services. The issue groups many sectors, each with one or two items.

The tax service now has an approved IT programme and a roadmap with a timetable, which is evidence of planning progress. Against that, the work spreads across many agencies and EU systems, and some connections depend on EU arrangements open only to Member States, as the government notes for the AGORA system.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since the issue comes from a cross-cutting theme and its items sit in the economic sections. The Commission finds digitalisation lagging behind in 2023, slowly improving in 2024, steadily advancing in 2025 and continuing to advance in 2026, but these findings concern the economy as a whole. Across all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, the only repeated measure of business adoption is the Government's share of enterprises making web sales, 0.9% both in its 2023 strategy and as the baseline of its 2025 programme, so no item shows a change in business adoption itself.

Responses are in place: SME digitalisation programmes, association to the Digital Europe Programme and the first European Digital Innovation Hub, launched in April 2026. Against that, the Reform Agenda finds the share of businesses using digital services low, and the government's 2025 programme still gives a baseline of 0.9% of enterprises making web sales. What remains is wider adoption of digital technologies by small businesses and greater use of EU programmes and the new innovation hub.

The Commission's findings on this issue are general statements in the economic sections, positive since 2024, and a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on business adoption. Business adoption is not an acquis requirement.

Support programmes, EU funding routes and the first innovation hub exist, and the Commission records steady progress in digitalisation. Against that, adoption depends on many small firms, and the government cites lack of knowledge, high costs and perceived long-term returns as barriers.

The chapter scale was used as context only, since this is part of the chapter. The Commission finds about 40% of mapped services available digitally in 2024, over 50% in 2025 with 64% for businesses and 54% for individuals in 2024, and 82% of business services and 61% of citizen services by June 2026, and its 2026 release decision confirms that the Reform Agenda objective of 75% of business services was met. The 2026 report also finds that user uptake increased significantly, including in rural areas.

The business services reform is in place, with the State Register of Legal Units launched in December 2025 and the life events methodology approved, and the Commission judges the payment step satisfactorily fulfilled. Still, only 133 of the 414 business services counted are fully digital end to end, citizen services lag at 61%, the Commission noted low demand in 2025, and the systems of the entrepreneurship agency and the employment agency are still being procured or built. What remains is end-to-end online delivery and wider use of sector services, especially for citizens and in agencies such as the entrepreneurship and employment agencies.

Digital services for businesses are the subject of key recommendations in four reports: digitalising processes to cut administrative burden in 2023 and 2024, and digitalising the entrepreneurship agency's processes in 2025 and 2026. The related Reform Agenda payment step (75% of business services digitalised, with the State Register of Legal Units and the life events methodology) is met, so the rating rests on the repeated recommendations; online public services are central to the digital government theme.

There is strong evidence of past progress, with the share of business services online rising each year from 2024 to 2026 and the payment step met. The work is led by the e-Governance Agency and the State Chancellery with shared platforms, although sector agencies and rural demand still need attention.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since the issue comes from a cross-cutting theme. The Commission finds the e-procurement system inadequate in 2021, calls for it to be overhauled or re-engineered in 2023, describes MTender as outdated in 2025, and in 2026 records limited progress on digitalising procurement and an outdated MTender that limits monitoring; a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no item from the 2024 report on e-procurement.

The new system is still being procured: technical specifications were received in September 2025 and the call for bids was published in December 2025 with a deadline in February 2026, while the Reform Agenda sets a pilot of the new system by December 2027. MTender remains in use without planning, contract management and some procedures. What remains is designing, building and putting into operation a new e-procurement system that covers every procedure and stage of the procurement cycle.

The new e-procurement system is a Reform Agenda payment condition, recalled in the 2025 release decision, and the Commission calls for it in the 2023 report and in the key recommendations of the 2025 and 2026 reports. It is central to digital public procurement.

Funding from international partners is secured, a concept and programme exist, and procurement of the system has started with World Bank review. Against that, the system has been called for since 2021 with limited progress recorded in 2026, and building a full new system is a large technical project.

The Chapter 2 rating covers more than this issue and is context only, but its progress statements of 2024, 2025 and 2026 turn on the bilateral social security agreements, moving from limited progress in 2023 and 2024 to good progress in 2025 and 2026. The issue's own items show agreements added in each year: Spain signed and Greece in force by 2023, Spain and Latvia in force in 2024, Italy and France signed in October 2024 and March 2025, Italy in force in September 2025 and Slovakia signed in March 2026.

The Commission asked in each report from 2023 to 2026 for further social security coordination agreements with Member States, adding in 2026 a request for gap analyses on the coordination regulations, and it reports in 2026 that negotiations with other Member States should continue. The Government reported in 2025 agreements with 17 of the 27 Member States, its own count, and the Slovakia agreement signed in March 2026 is not yet reported in force. What remains is agreements with the Member States not yet covered, entry into force of those signed, and the gap analyses on the coordination regulations.

Concluding further agreements with Member States is a key recommendation in all four Commission reports from 2023 to 2026, and the Chapter 2 progress statements of 2024 to 2026 rest on it, so it is central to the chapter. Agreements have been added each year, but the recommendation is still repeated in 2026.

The Commission records agreements signed or brought into force in every year from 2023 to 2026, negotiated by an established institution, the National Social Insurance House. The Government itself says it cannot commit to a number of agreements because the pace depends on the political will of the other states, so completion is not in Moldova's hands alone.

The Chapter 2 rating covers more than this issue and is context only. The 2023 report and Analytical Report found the preparatory work for EURES not completed, the 2024 report recorded its start with an action plan and the National Employment Agency designated as coordination body, and the 2025 report recorded a EURES department and the September 2025 Government Decision setting the national legal framework. The 2026 report adds the National Coordination Office, the procedure for admitting members and partners, 10 territorial EURES members, implementing acts on data and monitoring and technical standards for matching with the EURES portal.

The Commission asked in 2023, 2024 and 2025 for the preparatory work for EURES to continue, and in 2026 it records the legal framework, coordination office and admission procedure as in place. The Government describes its 2024 and 2025 Decisions as only partial transposition of the EURES Regulation, says data exchange with the European platform and legislative alignment still need to be completed, and lists further agency orders, including on interoperability with EURES, as planned. What remains is completing legal alignment with the EURES Regulation and the technical connection and data exchange with the EURES platform, ahead of membership on accession.

Preparing to join EURES is a key recommendation in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and the 2026 key recommendation asks for the measures, capacity and IT systems needed for full participation in EURES, while the Commission states that the previous year's recommendations remain valid. The requirement therefore runs through four reports and joining EURES is central to the chapter, although the Commission records the main legal and organisational steps as taken in 2026.

The work lies mainly with one body, the National Employment Agency, and uses Government Decisions and agency orders; the steps planned in 2024 and 2025 were reported as taken by the Commission in the following report. The remaining technical connection depends on the employment service's IT capacity, which the 2025 recommendation asks Moldova to reinforce.

Across all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, the EU items on the European Health Insurance Card concern its domestic preconditions: the 2025 sub-area wording records no progress on the Card and the 2026 report a feasibility study and an action plan, and these are used for the issue on those preconditions. None states whether EU citizens can obtain healthcare in Moldova with the Card, and the Government stated in 2025 that the EU acts on the Card are not transposed, so two points in time with no assessed change in access are not enough to set a direction.

The Government stated in 2025 that the EU acts on the European Health Insurance Card are not transposed and listed applying the Card and a draft law on cross-border medical care as planned. In 2026 the Commission reported a feasibility study on the Card, finalised in August 2026, and an EHIC Action Plan approved the same month. What remains is a decision on introducing the Card and the legal and financial arrangements that would give EU citizens access to healthcare through it.

The Card is part of the Chapter 2 acquis on social security coordination and is named in the key recommendations of the 2025 and 2026 reports, as IT infrastructure and capacity for the EHIC scheme to be developed alongside the Electronic Exchange of Social Security Information. Two reports fall short of the three-report test, which keeps it below High.

Preparation has started: a feasibility study on the Card's impact on public finances was completed and a draft law on cross-border medical care is planned. The study's focus on public finances points to cost as the main constraint, and the international cooperation section dealing with Member State institutions has three specialists.

The issue rests on a single item, found by a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files for personal data in elections and campaigns: a 2026 civil society report that illegal surveys in the parliamentary election campaign used personal data databases of unclear origin. No EU item raises it, and one item from one year cannot show a direction.

The single item is a civil society finding, and no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files states an EU requirement on it or describes an intervention responding to it, so the gap cannot be measured against what the EU requires. What remains is, on that one report, oversight of how personal data are obtained, stored and used in election campaigns, which other sources would need to confirm.

The issue is raised only by one civil society source, the single item on it among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, and not in EU material, which keeps priority from being High. With no EU recommendation or benchmark, it is Low.
The single item names no responsible institution and no past action on the issue, so how realistic progress would be cannot be judged.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only, as this issue comes from a cross-cutting theme and was not decisive. SIGMA found in 2023 that government websites complied poorly with WCAG 2.0 despite guidelines, with an average of 45 errors per page across 26 tested sites, and the Commission found in 2026 that public sector websites and mobile applications remain insufficiently accessible and that accessibility is insufficiently enforced and funded.

The 2026 key recommendation asks Moldova to improve the accessibility of public sector websites and mobile applications. The law on accessibility requirements for products and services adopted in August 2026, which the Commission describes as in line with the acquis, is a legal step for products and services, while the order setting WCAG 2.2 rules for public websites had not started in 2026 because it awaits a Government Decision. What remains is binding accessibility rules for public sector websites and applications and their enforcement and funding.

Accessibility of public sector websites and applications is a key recommendation in the 2026 report, the first Commission report to raise it in a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, and no Reform Agenda payment condition names it. It is a clear EU requirement but not yet repeated across reports.

Guidelines for government websites already exist, and the WCAG 2.2 rules are a single order of the e-Governance Agency once the Government Decision is approved. The poor compliance SIGMA found across many sites in 2023 and the Commission's finding that accessibility is insufficiently enforced and funded show that bringing existing sites into line needs resources across many institutions.

Sub-area wording on the 5G Cybersecurity Toolbox, which matches this issue, recorded no progress in 2024. The Commission asked in 2025 for implementation of the Toolbox measures to continue and in 2026 for Moldova to start implementing them, including restrictions on high-risk suppliers, so the core requirement is unchanged across the three reports; the secondary legislation on security of public 5G networks noted in 2026 and the supplier risk study under way are preparatory steps.

The 2026 report asks Moldova to start implementing the Toolbox measures, including restrictions or exclusions for high-risk suppliers, which the Reform Agenda also sets as a step. The Government reports a supplier risk assessment by a consultancy still in progress and a draft Government Decision on 5G network security still being finalised in 2026, with a 5G security law planned by December 2027. What remains is the 5G security law, the completed supplier risk assessment and restrictions on high-risk suppliers applied to critical assets.

Alignment with the 5G Toolbox is part of the key recommendation on the Digital Transformation Strategy priorities in the 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports and is a step of the Reform Agenda under the Reform and Growth Facility, after the sub-area recorded no progress in 2024. It is central to the cybersecurity theme.

Funded preparatory work is under way, with a study funded by Swedfund and a consultancy contract covering supplier risk assessment, an operator compensation mechanism and a draft law. The Government notes that compliance requires major investment in 5G networks, so progress depends on operators bearing, or being compensated for, the cost of restricting high-risk suppliers.

The Chapter 29 rating covers more than this issue and is context only; it recorded good progress in 2025 and 2026, naming the New Computerised Transit System both times. The issue's own items move from uncertainty about the transit system in 2021 and requests for an IT strategy in 2023 and 2024, to migration to NCTS Phase 5 in October 2024, Phase 6 in September 2025, full accession to the Common Transit Convention in November 2025 and a fully operational Customs Decisions System by June 2026.

The 2026 report asks Moldova to adopt the Customs Code amendments that give the legal basis for EU-interoperable IT systems and to advance the national customs IT programme approved in October 2025, of whose 25 systems three are operational. The Commission notes that implementation remains incomplete because of transitional provisions and a lack of IT tools, and the Government states that the programme has no budget coverage. What remains is the Customs Code amendments and most of the programme's systems, including the core interconnectivity systems and a Single Window Environment for Customs.

Customs IT is a key recommendation in every Commission report from 2023 to 2026, and accession to the Common Transit Convention, the transit system and the Customs Decisions System are steps of the Reform Agenda. Interoperability with the EU electronic customs environment is central to the customs chapter and to the interoperability theme.

The Customs Service delivered the transit system, Convention accession and the Customs Decisions System close to the dates set, the Commission judged the related Reform Agenda steps satisfactorily fulfilled, and EU expert support continues. The lack of budget coverage for the 2025 to 2030 programme, reported by the Government, is the main risk to keeping that pace.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only, as this issue is part of the AI theme and the scale was not decisive. The Government recorded a lack of legal acts on AI in 2023, the Commission found in 2025 that Moldova is not yet aligned with the AI Act and in 2026 asked it to develop governance, regulatory and enforcement structures, and the Government's 2026 programme document still describes the field as at an early stage with no competent authority or AI-specific framework. The 2024 White Paper is declarative, and a 2026 civil society report says the AI sub-council produced no legislative initiative.

The Commission requires governance, regulatory and enforcement structures in line with the AI Act. A draft AI law, a law on AI testing spaces, the 2026 to 2030 national programme and an AI governance institution are all planned or being drafted, and the Government reported in 2025 that no institution responsible for AI policy or supervision had been identified. What remains is a law aligned with the AI Act, a designated and staffed supervisory authority, and the governance structure to apply it.

AI Act alignment is raised by the Commission in 2025 as a finding and in 2026 as a recommendation, and a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found it in no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition. It is central to the AI theme but not yet repeated across three reports.

The National Accession Programme plans transposition of the AI Act and a governance institution by 2027, and a consultative sub-council exists. In 2025 no ministry employee covered AI policy, the competent authority was yet to be chosen, and funding for the national programme depends on the annual budget process.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only. The Commission found the 2022 law partially aligned with eIDAS in 2023, found full alignment with eIDAS 1.0 in 2025 with the European Digital Identity framework to follow, and in 2026 found an advanced level of alignment after the December 2025 amendments on qualified trust service providers. The improvement is legal, and sources conflict on when Law No. 124/2022 entered into force: 10 December 2022 in the 2023 report, 1 January 2025 according to the Government.

The Commission asked in 2024 for interoperability with the European Digital Identity Wallets, and the Reform Agenda expects alignment with eIDAS 2 and an EU-aligned national wallet by December 2026. In 2026 the law transposing eIDAS 2 was still being drafted, a set of implementing orders on the wallet framework was planned, and the national wallet was under development since September 2025. What remains is the eIDAS 2 law and its implementing acts, and a national digital identity wallet interoperable with the European Digital Identity Wallets.

Alignment with EU electronic identification requirements was part of the 2024 key recommendation, and alignment with eIDAS 2 with an EU-aligned national wallet is a step of the Reform Agenda due by December 2026. It is central to the electronic identification theme.

Moldova moved from partial to advanced alignment between 2023 and 2026, with amending laws in 2025 and technical assistance under EU4Digital for eIDAS 2. Staffing is thin, with one ministry post on trust services and the capacity of the ministry and regulator named as needs, which may slow the remaining implementing acts.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only. The 2023 report recorded adoption of the Law on cybersecurity but said implementation had to start, the 2024 and 2025 reports recorded implementing Government Decisions aimed at NIS 2 alignment, and the 2026 report records further secondary legislation and the National Cybersecurity Programme 2026-2030 adopted in December 2025, replacing the strategy the Reform Agenda had described as lapsed. The improvement is mainly legal and strategic, as the Reform Agenda still found no holistic framework in 2025.

The key recommendation of 2024, 2025 and 2026 asks Moldova to align legislation with EU cybersecurity standards. The Government describes Law No. 48/2023 as only partially harmonising with NIS 2, and the amending law for NIS 2, the laws on the Cyber Resilience Act and cybersecurity certification and the related authority designations were still planned in 2025 and 2026. What remains is full transposition of NIS 2 and of the Cyber Resilience Act and certification framework, with the authorities designated to apply them.

Alignment with EU cybersecurity standards is in the key recommendation of the 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, and NIS 2 alignment with clarified institutional roles is part of the Reform Agenda. The legal framework is central to the cybersecurity theme.

Moldova has adopted the main law and a series of implementing Government Decisions since 2023, which shows legislative capacity. The Cybersecurity Agency reports that missing staff and an incomplete framework limited supervision in 2025, the ministry's cybersecurity unit has four posts with one vacant, and the Reform Agenda expects compliance costs to meet resistance from operators.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only. In 2021 the national CERT was pending approval of its mandate, in 2024 and 2025 the Commission asked for further effort on the operational capacity of the new Cybersecurity Agency, and the Reform Agenda found it short of staff, IT resources and legal authority. In 2026 the Commission reports the Agency operational as single point of contact and national CERT, with 32 staff by December 2025 and an incident platform in use, and judged the related Reform Agenda step satisfactorily fulfilled.

The Reform Agenda step on making the Agency fully operational with a national CERT is judged fulfilled, but the Agency's 2025 report says supervision was only partly carried out for lack of staff and a complete framework, its SIEM and incident playbooks were incomplete, and it lacks qualified IT specialists. The Government reports that cyber incidents rose by over 30 percent between 2021 and 2023, and the 2026 report notes security vulnerabilities in the border police information system. What remains is enough qualified staff and tools for the Agency and CERT to supervise providers and protect state systems.

Operational capacity of the Agency was named in the 2024 and 2025 reports and in a Reform Agenda step, but the Commission judged that step satisfactorily fulfilled, and a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no 2026 Commission recommendation on the Agency's capacity. A fulfilled condition with no repeat of the requirement in 2026 does not on its own make the issue High, although it stays central to the cybersecurity theme.

The Agency went from its launch in 2024 to an operational CERT in 2025, with substantial EU and bilateral support in experts, equipment, software and training. The Agency names recruitment of qualified specialists and limited own resources for equipment as its constraints.

The Commission's 2023 analytical report found that the law on access to the labour market made no difference between EU workers and other third-country nationals, and the 2024 report recorded amendments letting EU citizens work without a work permit. The 2025 report recorded a law of July 2025 giving EU citizens a separate regime, and the 2026 report the entry into force in March 2026 of the law on free movement and residence of EU citizens, aimed at alignment; the improvement is legal only. The chapter rating (early stage in 2023 and 2024, some level in 2025, between some and moderate in 2026) covers the whole chapter and was used as context only.

Law No. 200/2025, in force since March 2026, gives EU citizens a regime separate from other foreigners and, by the government's account, equal treatment with nationals, but the 2026 key recommendation still asks for continued alignment on access to the labour market and equal treatment of EU workers. The amendments to the employment law and its implementing decision, the adjustment of secondary legislation by several ministries and the removal of the citizenship condition for staff of private employment agencies are still at draft or planning stage. What remains is secondary and sectoral legislation giving EU workers equal access to employment services, active measures, service housing and private placement, and its application in practice.

Access for EU citizens to the labour market and equal treatment are central to the chapter and are named in the key recommendations of the 2025 and 2026 reports, but not in those of 2023 or 2024, so the test of three or more reports is not met. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on the issue; the 2023 report also contains a general call to align legislation with the acquis, outside its key recommendations.

The remaining work is national legislation and staff training led by the Ministry of Labour and other ministries, and the drafts are already prepared and under consultation. Past progress is clear: the Commission reports amendments in force from January 2024 and Law No. 200/2025 in force from March 2026.

In 2023 the Commission found that EU citizens needed a temporary residence permit for work and that their family members were treated as other foreigners, while the 2023 report recorded amendments easing temporary residence for EU citizens; the 2024 report recorded amendments in force from January 2024 letting them work without a work permit. The 2025 report recorded a separate regime for EU citizens, and the 2026 report the entry into force of the free movement law in March 2026 and a standard operating procedure for their residence documents; the improvement is mainly legal. The chapter rating covers the whole chapter and was used as context only.

Under Law No. 200/2025 EU citizens need no work authorisation and, for stays over 90 days, a residence card not tied to a purpose, but the Commission reports that only 28 applications for the new residence documents had been submitted after the March 2026 procedure, while 422 EU citizens were still to be documented under the old stay-for-work regime in 2025. Full separation of the two regimes in the general law on foreigners depends on a draft law due to apply from 1 June 2027, and the Ministry of Internal Affairs' secondary legislation on registering EU citizens is still being revised. What remains is the practical move of EU citizens and their family members to the new residence cards and the completion of the implementing rules.

Work permits and residence conditions for EU workers are central to the chapter, but they are not named separately in a key recommendation; the 2025 and 2026 key recommendations on access for EU citizens to the labour market can be read as covering them, which would still make only two reports. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on the issue.

The legal change has been made and the General Inspectorate for Migration has an operating procedure, so what is left is mostly administrative and within national control. Few EU citizens had applied for the new documents by 2026, and full separation of the regimes depends on a new foreigners law that is still a draft, so progress depends on the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Inspectorate following through.

The issue is first raised in the Commission's 2025 key recommendation to reinforce the employment service's IT infrastructure for EURES, when the 2025 report also recorded a new EURES department with a designated officer from January 2025. The 2026 report records technical standards for matching vacancies and CVs with the EURES portal and a new integrated information system developed in December 2025, aiming at fully digitalised services by 2027, while widening the recommendation to systems for EESSI and the EHIC. The chapter rating was not decisive, as the issue is only part of the chapter.

The employment agency has a Labour Migration and EURES directorate (five of six posts filled) and technical standards for exchange with the EURES portal, but the interoperability of its information system with EURES, staff training on EURES and the rules on personal data in that exchange are still planned. The agency's own reports for 2024 and 2025 say it lacks a modern information system, and the new system, funded through the EU Delegation, is still being developed. What remains is a working connection between the agency's information system and the EURES platform, operated by trained staff, before accession.

The employment service's IT capacity for EURES is named in the key recommendations of the 2025 and 2026 reports, two reports, and supports a chapter requirement that applies from accession. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on it.

The work sits mainly with one agency, which has already set up a EURES directorate and technical standards, so there is evidence of past progress. The new information system depends on external funding and on technical connection work that is still planned, and the agency reports unfilled posts within its staff ceiling.

The issue is not raised as a Chapter 2 finding or requirement in EU material: across all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, the Commission items on third-country nationals record the temporary residence rule and counts of residence permits, and its 2023 call to register foreigners and give them access to services sits under Chapter 24, so the standard scale was not decisive. The issue's own items describe continuing barriers to third-country workers' access from 2024 to 2026: the migration inspectorate's 2024 proposals to remove problems found in the foreigners law, a 2025 study finding the procedure for employing foreigners bureaucratic, and UNHCR's 2026 finding that only 29 percent of working-age Ukrainian refugees are in paid work, with language, recognition of qualifications and childcare as barriers. The new law on admission of foreigners that would change the rules is a draft due to apply from June 2027.

No EU item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files states a Chapter 2 requirement on third-country workers, so the gap is judged on the issue's own items. The draft law on admission of foreigners and the draft amendment extending employment services to more categories of foreigners are proposals, and consultation comments on the draft law point to work permits tied to one employer and no clear separation between labour inspection and immigration control, while refugees still face language, recognition and childcare barriers. What remains is a law in force that eases third-country workers' access to the labour market and protects their rights after admission, and support that reaches refugees in practice.

The issue is not raised as a requirement in EU material, which counts residence permits and records the residence rules, and this keeps priority from being High: a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no Commission recommendation on third-country workers' access to the labour market, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition, and the 2023 Chapter 24 recommendation on registering foreigners and giving them access to services does not concern employment. The evidence comes from national, international organisation and research sources, which do not raise priority.

A full draft law on admission of foreigners and a draft amendment to the employment law have been prepared and consulted, and the employment agency already supports refugees with partner organisations. Against that, the barriers named by UNHCR (language, recognition of diplomas, childcare) need several ministries and funding, and the draft law would apply only from June 2027.

Only two items fall under this issue: a 2021 Commission finding on use of the online tender platform for COVID-19 procurement and a 2023 report of a regulation requiring most low-value procurement to go through the State Registry of Public Procurement system. Across all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, the findings that MTender lacks planning and contract management modules and does not offer all procedures concern the replacement of the system and are held under that issue, so no sequence can be drawn on fuller use of the existing modules, and the chapter rating was not used.

No item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files states an EU requirement on fuller use of the existing e-procurement modules or on use of procurement data for red-flag analysis, or reports use of the low-value procurement module required by the 2023 regulation; the Commission's requirements on MTender concern its replacement by a new system. What remains is not known from the evidence held.

A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no Commission recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on fuller use of the existing e-procurement modules, since those on MTender concern a new system, and the 2021 finding concerns the transparency of emergency procurement rather than the electronic tools themselves.
The two items on this issue say nothing about the actors, costs or obstacles involved in fuller use of the e-procurement modules, so tractability cannot be judged.

A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found that the Commission's only items on these tools are two 2023 calls, in the analytical report and the 2023 report, for electronic platforms and procedures alongside legal alignment on professional qualifications, with no later EU assessment of them. The government's 2025 plans to reconfigure the public services portal as the point of single contact and to link the National Register of Qualifications with Europass are planned and under way respectively, so there is no sequence to judge.

The 2023 Commission calls for electronic platforms and procedures are met so far only by plans: reconfiguring the public services portal as the point of single contact is planned, and making the National Register of Qualifications interoperable with Europass is under way. What remains is a point of single contact giving service providers full online information and procedures, and an electronic register of regulated professions and qualifications.

The Commission's calls for electronic platforms in this area appear only in 2023, as part of wider recommendations on professional qualifications, and their link to the technology theme is uncertain; a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on them.

The public services portal already works and could be reconfigured, and the work lies with national bodies. Against that, one measure is planned and one under way, the government expects possible problems of interoperability with EU platforms, and no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files reports past progress on either; the Government describes the EVO portal as a one-stop shop for public services in general, not as the point of single contact for service providers.

In 2023 the Commission reported that 67.5% of households had internet at home (58% in rural areas), in 2025 that high-speed broadband reached 57% of the population by mid-2024 while regional disparities persisted, and in 2026 that nearly 95% of households had internet access. The 2026 sub-area wording on 5G deployment, which matches this part of the issue, is some progress, with coverage of 25 to 35%; the Chapter 10 rating was used as context only, as the issue is part of the chapter.

Coverage and take-up have risen, and the Commission's assessment for the third Reform and Growth Facility release records 6.9% more fixed-broadband connections and faster speeds between 2025 and 2026, but 5G coverage remains well below the EU average and the Reform Agenda describes a rural-urban digital divide. The government counts 431 localities in white areas without fixed broadband, and the plan to develop networks there is proposed and waits for the regulator's geographic survey. What remains is high-capacity fixed and 5G coverage in rural and small localities.

The rural-urban digital divide is named in a 2024 economic key recommendation on infrastructure investment, the Reform Agenda describes it and the 2026 report rates 5G deployment, but a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no Chapter 10 key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on coverage. The related Reform Agenda step concerns alignment with the Electronic Communications Code, which belongs to another issue.

Spectrum was awarded through competitions in 2024 and 2025, operators are investing and the Commission records progress on 5G, which is evidence of past progress. Closing the remaining gaps depends on private operators and on public funding for small, isolated localities, which the government says require significant investment.

In 2021 the draft data protection law had been awaiting second reading since 2018, and in 2023 the Commission found the law only to some extent aligned with the GDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive. The 2024 report recorded adoption of the GDPR law, the 2025 report its entry into force due in August 2026, and the 2026 report its entry into force, the adoption in August 2026 of a law aligning with the Law Enforcement Directive and ratification of the second protocol to Convention 108; the improvement is legal only. The Chapter 10 rating was not decisive, as the issue spans several chapters.

The main laws the Commission has called for since 2023 are now adopted, but the 2026 report says Moldova should still implement EU standards on contractual clauses between operators and processors, and the 2026 key recommendation still asks for further alignment with EU data protection standards. The order on standard contractual clauses exists only as a draft, and beyond the 2024 and 2026 laws no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files reports the review of related national laws that the 2023 report described as pending since 2020 and the World Bank recommended in 2024. What remains is the rules on standard contractual clauses and the alignment of related national laws with the new data protection laws.

Alignment of data protection legislation is named in the Chapter 10 key recommendations of the 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, after the 2023 report called for the data protection law to be amended, and it is central to the data theme. A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no Reform Agenda payment condition on it.

Moldova adopted the GDPR law in 2024 and, in 2026, the law enforcement data protection law and the ratification of the Convention 108 protocol, which is strong evidence of past progress. What is left is mainly an order on contractual clauses, already drafted, and the alignment of related national laws with the new data protection laws, both within the government's control.

A search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files for the Interoperable Europe Act and the European Interoperability Framework found no Commission finding or recommendation on the national framework's alignment; the EU items are a Growth Plan support measure and a 2026 note that the open data law is in line with the European Interoperability Framework. The government stated in 2025 that the national framework follows the Framework's principles but that the Interoperable Europe Act is not transposed, and drafting of the amending law was announced in February 2026, which is too short a record to show a direction.

By the government's own account the Interoperable Europe Act has not been transposed, and the law amending Law No. 142/2018 to do so was only initiated in February 2026; the Interoperable Europe factsheet notes that Moldova is not yet part of the European Interoperability Framework data collection. What remains is transposition of the Interoperable Europe Act into the data exchange and interoperability law and alignment of the national framework with the latest European Interoperability Framework.

The issue is not raised as a requirement in the Commission's reports or the Reform Agenda: a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no such item, which keeps priority from being High. It rests on the government's own gap analysis and an EU support measure under the Growth Plan.

The change is one amendment to an existing law, prepared by the government, and Moldova already has a working legal and technical interoperability framework. Drafting began only in February 2026, and no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files shows progress beyond the February 2026 drafting notice.

The Commission reported in 2023 that data exchange through MConnect let the electoral commission check party financing more effectively, but in 2025 it said interoperability between automated verification systems and state registries must still be strengthened, and in 2026 it noted constraints on the full practical functioning of interoperable verification tools. Other sources show connections continuing (336 institutions in 2023 according to SIGMA; 396 integrated state and private systems in 2025 according to the Government, a different measure) while the same underuse is reported: the World Bank in 2024 found interoperability yet to be streamlined, the government in 2025 found systems fragmented, and the data protection authority in 2026 found state bodies still using COI access outside the platform. The Chapter 10 rating was not decisive, as the issue is cross-cutting.

The platform and the legal duty to exchange data through it are in place, with sanctions since 2021, and SIGMA found the base registers connected to it in 2023. The data protection authority finds that state bodies still access personal data through COI technology outside the platform, which conflicts with the government's statement that data exchange takes place exclusively through MConnect, and the Commission in 2026 still finds the interoperable verification tools for asset declarations not fully functioning. What remains is regular use of the platform by all institutions, including an end to access outside it, and full data exchange for asset declaration checks.

Interoperability for asset declaration checks is part of a Chapter 23 Reform Agenda step on the new e-Integrity system, with interoperability ensured through MConnect, is named in the 2025 main findings on Chapter 23 and is repeated as a finding in 2026. These EU items concern only asset declaration checks, and a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark, key recommendation or Reform Agenda payment condition on use of the platform as a whole, although regular use of the platform is central to the interoperability theme.

The platform, the law and sanctions already exist and connections have grown, which is evidence of past progress. Against that, the remaining problem lies with many institutions that the World Bank says work in silos, and the data protection authority reports that bodies notified repeatedly have still not moved to the platform.

The Commission found in 2025 that Moldova was not yet fully aligned with the Chips Act and in 2026 that it was yet to align with it. The 2026 sub-area wording on semiconductors, which matches this issue, is some progress, but it rests on the April 2026 law on topographies of semiconductor products, an intellectual property matter outside the issue, so alignment with the Chips Act has not moved.

The 2026 key recommendation asks for further alignment with the semiconductor acquis, and the government plans to transpose the Chips Act by the end of 2026 but states that there are no national rules on semiconductor production facilities and no responsible institution. What remains is transposition of the Chips Act and the designation and staffing of a competent authority.

Alignment with the semiconductor acquis is a key recommendation in the 2026 report, following a 2025 finding, but only in one report, and a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on it. The government describes the sector in Moldova as almost non-existent, which makes the issue less central to the theme.

The government reports that no institution is responsible for the area, that no ministry employee covers it and that a new post is needed, and the sector is at an early stage. Transposition is planned for the end of 2026, but no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files records progress on the Chips Act itself.

Against its own targets, the strategy failed on services online (12% against 100%) and acceptance (49% against 70%), and the Commission links the shortfall to limited money and capacity. The Commission finds the strategy as a whole only partly successful, with 6 of 12 targets met, and the Government's 2023 Strategy agrees that the e-government objectives were not fully achieved, so this is not government reporting alone.

The Commission measures the shortfall against the strategy's own targets and names causes (limited money, project management and implementation capacity), so the link is direct. The figures describe the state of services rather than an isolated effect of the strategy.

The Government reports a higher share of digitalised services and 70% of business service requests online in 2023, and the Commission independently records notable progress on digitalising public services in 2024 and 64% of business and 54% of citizen services online in 2024. The result is narrow: it concerns availability and business use, and citizen services lag.

The Commission ties progress to continued implementation of the Strategy, but digitalisation was already under way through earlier projects, and the Strategy was adopted only in September 2023. Government counts of 2023 business requests also differ between its 2024 and 2025 documents.

The Commission reports a significant rise in uptake, including in rural areas where the centres were set up, but gives no rural figure and does not say the centres caused it, and the centres' own service counts come from Government sources. None of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources measures use of the centres.
The sentence places the centres beside the rise in uptake rather than stating that they produced it, and a wider rise in online use is reported nationally over the same period.

The only evidence is the e-Governance Agency's own anniversary publication: none of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources measures delivery times of the redesigned services, so success is not judged from government reporting alone.
None of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources measures the outcome, so there is nothing independent to which the project could be attributed.

The doubling of use comes from the e-Governance Agency's own publication, so success is not judged from government reporting alone: none of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources measures use over the project period, and the Commission's figures on rising use do not mention the project.

The publication links the rise to the project, but use rose with many parallel measures, including EVO and the service centres, and none of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources separates the project's effect.

This figure comes from the e-Governance Agency's own publication, which the Agency reports as its own view, and none of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources measures access by vulnerable groups, so success is not judged from government reporting alone.
None of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources measures access by vulnerable groups or links it to the project.

The savings claim comes from the e-Governance Agency's own publication, with no method given, and none of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources estimates savings from MPay, so success is not judged from government reporting alone.
None of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources estimates the savings, so there is nothing independent to which MPay could be attributed.

The Court of Accounts, an audit body independent of the e-Governance Agency, confirms the register works and that 67 authorities had registered 88 systems, but rates its recommendation only partly implemented, finds registration delayed and 63% of registered systems not properly documented (machine translated). SIGMA states that all systems were registered, which conflicts with the Court's finding.
The outcome is use of the register itself, counted from the system's own statistics, so it cannot have another source.

The only evidence is the regulator's own annual report, machine translated: none of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources assesses the effect of the BEREC working arrangements, so success is not judged.
The statement describes expected benefits from the moment of signing rather than an observed change in the regulator's work.

The 100% reporting rate comes from a Government monitoring report (machine translated), and none of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources measures reporting through the platform, so success is not judged from government reporting alone. The platform serves internal control reporting, so its link to the technology theme is uncertain.
The reports were submitted through the platform after its user group was extended in 2025, so the link is direct, but reporting was a legal obligation that may have been met by other means before.

The Commission finds the strategy only partially successful, with 6 of 12 targets met, and attributes the shortfall to limited funding and weak project management and implementation capacity. The Government's final report likewise finds e-government objectives not fully achieved despite developments.

The outcome is measured against the strategy's own targets and the Commission links the results to its implementation. Targets such as ICT sector growth also depend on factors outside the strategy, and none of the five items of this run on the Digital Moldova 2020 strategy, found by a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files, separates them.

The Court of Accounts, an external auditor, finds that the agency's procurement opinions created conditions to secure the State's rights over systems, but rates the related recommendation only partly implemented. It also finds the methodology unamended from 2021 to August 2024, the agency not always involved in procurement and spending still not traceable.
The auditor attributes the outcome directly to the agency's coordination of ICT procurement, citing the opinions it issued that require public entities to hold source code and ownership rights.

The Commission reports tangible benefits from the voluntary arrangements, and an independent civil society source reports that all Moldovan mobile operators launched offers with significantly reduced tariffs from the start of 2024.
The lower roaming prices are the direct content of the agreement, which set reduced tariffs from January 2024, and the Commission links the benefits to the arrangements it facilitated.
The source reports reduced roaming tariffs offered by all mobile operators in 30 EU and EEA countries from the start of 2024, which the Commission also reports as tangible benefits.
The reduced offers began on the date the agreement set for lower tariffs, and the agreement's purpose was to lower those tariffs.

The fall in the roaming basket and the rise in traffic come from a report of the two countries' national regulators, relayed by a civil society source without separate verification. No other item among the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources confirms the effect.

The source places the price fall after the February 2022 agreement and the agreement concerns roaming tariffs, but it reports no comparison that would separate the agreement from other market changes.
The Commission states that roaming charges were removed and immediate benefits reached citizens and businesses, and the 2026 report confirms that Moldova joined Roam Like at Home on 1 January 2026.
Removal of roaming charges is the defining effect of joining the area, and the Commission links it directly to the extension of Roam Like at Home to Moldova.

The outcome is legal: the Government's statement that the legislative preconditions were created is confirmed by the Commission, which found the roaming acquis correctly transposed in full and admitted Moldova to Roam Like at Home on that basis.

The roaming law is one of the acts the Commission assessed as transposing the roaming acquis, together with secondary acts and the Association Council decision, so it is a direct contributor to the legal outcome.
The law entered into force only on 1 January 2026, and the Commission describes the alignment as facilitating roll-out, which is an expected effect rather than an observed one.

The Commission attributes the facilitation to all the alignment together, including roaming and infrastructure access measures, and does not link the reported growth in fixed broadband connections and speeds to the law.
The claimed gains in capacity and 5G roll-out come only from the regulator's own annual report on its own competitions, and no independent item among the Moldova items on this issue measures them.
Licensed spectrum is a precondition for the capacity and 5G services described, so the link is plausible, but deployment also depends on operators' investment, which the source does not separate.

The Commission, an independent source, states that information exchanges through SIENA increased after its roll-out to several law enforcement bodies, which is the result the 2023 recommendation sought. No figures are given.
The outcome is use of the system itself, so it can only come from the roll-out.

The outcome item is a general civil society statement with no measure of datasets published or re-used, and across all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files the only count of datasets is the Government's single figure of 1,268 on the portal; adoption of the law alone is not success.
The source names the law together with training and improvements to the participation platform as causes, so the law is one of several.

The claim rests on government reporting alone: none of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources measures funds won with the contact point's help, and the related figures are applications and institutions assisted rather than funds won.
The source asserts the link without evidence that separates the contact point's help from other factors.
The Commission states the payments system is helping small entrepreneurs, but gives no measure of costs or business use.
The Commission names the payments system together with the expansion of online trade platforms, so it is one of two causes.

The claim rests on government reporting alone, without figures: none of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources links signature use to the health system, and the Commission gives electronic signature use at about 10% of adults in both 2024 and 2025.
The source states the link but gives no data that separate the effect of the health system from other drivers of signature use.
The Commission, an independent source, states that user uptake of e-services increased significantly, including in rural areas, after the Commission had noted low demand in 2025.
The Commission places the centres beside the rise in uptake but does not say the rise is due to them, and other services expanded in the same period.

The Court of Accounts, an audit body, records improved accessibility of permit services, but the same audit finds only partial use of the system, reluctance by some authorities and major risks that its purpose will not be achieved.
The outcome concerns the system's own use and the services it automates.
The Commission verified that 310 of 414 business services are digitalised, meeting the 75% objective, though only 133 are fully digital end to end.
The reform is the framework for the objective, but the Commission already gave 64% of business services online in 2024, so much of the result predates it.

The claim of significant progress in 2023 rests on the Government's own report: the Commission gives about 40% of services available online in both its 2023 and 2024 reports, which does not show the rise, and its higher figures concern 2024 and later. The Strategy was also adopted only in September 2023.

The Strategy was adopted in September 2023, so most of the 2023 results the Government reports predate it, and Government counts of 2023 business service requests differ between its 2024 and 2025 documents.

The claim rests on government reporting alone: none of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources refers to the services digitalised through the project in 2023, and the count is of services digitalised rather than their use.

The only statement that the services were digitalised through the project is the Government's own implementation report, and none of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources refers to the project's 2023 output, so its contribution cannot be judged on independent evidence.

The Commission reports that full accession to the Common Transit Convention followed in November 2025 and that the interoperability of customs operations was significantly enhanced, and it records NCTS Phase 6 connected to the common transit network. This is an independent EU finding of an effect beyond the system's launch.

The Commission links the Convention accession and interoperability directly to the rollout of the transit system, which is the technical condition for connecting to the common transit network. Accession also needed legal and other technical steps, so the system was a necessary contributor rather than the only cause.

The claim of better social protection for Moldovans working abroad comes from the Government alone, and no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files measures coverage or benefits paid under the agreements. Signing and entry into force are not success.
The Government asserts the effect of its own agreements without data, so contribution cannot be confirmed beyond the general purpose of coordination agreements.

The statement of substantial progress towards a resilient cyber ecosystem is the Government's own; the Commission confirms the EU donation of equipment and licences and an operational Agency and CERT, but not the wider resilience the Government claims.
Several donors supported the Agency in the same period, including EUPM, TAIEX, Sweden, the OSCE and Estonia, so the share due to this project cannot be separated on the Government's statement alone.

The Commission, independent of the government, states that data exchange through MConnect enabled the Central Electoral Commission to check political party financing more effectively. The result is narrow and the report gives no measure of it.
The Commission states the causal link directly and names no other cause for the more effective checks.

The impact the audit records is that legal conditions were created for data exchange between the two systems, which is a legal step and not a result, and the audit was given no evidence that the exchange had been carried out or works.

The Court of Accounts, independent of the bodies audited, ties the legal conditions to the actions taken, but the outcome is itself only a legal condition and the audit also notes risks in the use of the systems.

Only the regulator reports the expansion of Moldtelecom's 4G coverage: among the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources, the 4G figures are national (nearly the entire population covered in the Commission's 2023 report, 99.3% in 2024 according to CSO Meter) and none measures a change after the award.
The regulator states that the expansion is due to the sub-1 GHz spectrum, which fits the stated mechanism of better propagation, but it is the regulator's account of its own action.

The spectrum was awarded in January 2025 and again during 2025, and the Commission records some progress on 5G deployment in 2026 with coverage of 25 to 35%, still well below the EU average, so roll-out is still under way.

None of the 1,451 Moldova items of this run from EU, international, civil society or research sources ties 5G progress to the competitions: the Commission records some progress on 5G deployment without naming them, and operators' own investment plans also drive roll-out.
The Commission states that the alignment facilitates roll-out, which is an expected effect rather than an observed one, and the law entered into force only on 1 January 2026.

The Commission attributes the easier roll-out to all the alignment together, including roaming and infrastructure access measures, and does not attribute the growth in fixed-broadband connections and speeds recorded in the same assessment to the law; with the law in force only since January 2026, its effect cannot be separated from earlier trends.
